{{margin-top:450px}}
# Part III: Religion
## Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended
### 13.1 Overview of the Pantheon


The gods of Tirvandor are real, present forces that grant power to their
faithful and occasionally manifest in the world. They are called "The
Seven Ascended" because ancient texts suggest they were once mortal
heroes who transcended to divinity during the Age of Dawn---ordinary
beings who achieved something extraordinary and became something
greater.

However, the gods are not all-knowing or all-powerful. They have
limitations, conflicts, and mysteries of their own. The relationship
between mortals and the divine is complex, shaped by two pivotal events:
the Divine Silence of 2,400-2,200 BW, when the gods stopped answering
prayers entirely, and the Worldrend of Year 0, which may have been
partially divine in origin.

**Philosophy of Worship**

Most Tirvandorians recognize the existence of all seven gods but
actively worship one to three that align with their values, profession,
or circumstances. A farmer might primarily worship Sylvara for good
harvests while also praying to Sera when illness strikes and Kael before
a long journey to market. A soldier might follow Thandros primarily but
honor Mordain before battle.

\column

Temples often house shrines to multiple deities, allowing worshippers to
address whichever god suits their current need. Only clergy typically
serve one deity exclusively, though even this is not universal---some
priests serve the pantheon as a whole rather than any single member.

**The Ascension**

The circumstances of the Seven's Ascension remain debated. Most
religious scholars agree it occurred during the Age of Dawn, sometime
after the first human kingdoms arose but before the Age of Strife. The
gods themselves have never directly confirmed or denied the Ascension
narrative.

Some theologians believe the Seven were chosen by older, now-departed
gods to serve as shepherds of mortal races. Others argue they achieved
divinity through extraordinary deeds that resonated with fundamental
forces of the universe. A minority position holds that the Ascension
story is a myth and the Seven have always existed in their current form.

What is certain is that the Seven demonstrate personality, memory, and
growth---characteristics more consistent with beings who were once
mortal than with eternal cosmic forces. They remember favors and
slights. They form opinions about mortal affairs. They disagree with
each other, sometimes publicly.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

### 13.2 Thandros, The Lawbringer

![13.2 Thandros, The Lawbringer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/god-thandros-law-justice.jpg){width:325px}


**Full Name and Titles:** Thandros the Lawbringer, The Judge, Lord of
Order, The Oathkeeper, The First King

**Sphere of Influence:** Law, Justice, Order, Civilization, Oaths,
Contracts, Government

**Personality and Values**

Thandros embodies the ideal of lawful civilization. He believes that
order and structure are necessary for society to flourish, that chaos
leads to suffering, and that even imperfect laws are better than no laws
at all. He is not cruel, but he is unyielding---the law must be upheld
even when mercy might seem kinder.

His followers understand that Thandros values consistency above all. A
judge who applies the law harshly but fairly earns his favor; one who
bends the law even for compassionate reasons risks his displeasure.
Oaths sworn in his name are absolutely binding, and breaking them
invites consequences that may extend beyond death.

Thandros believes in hierarchy, clear chains of command, and proper
procedure. He values documentation, formal agreements, and transparent
governance. He despises corruption, bribery, and those who use positions
of power for personal gain rather than public service.

**Symbol and Holy Days**

His symbol is **golden scales balanced on a sword**---representing
justice enforced by authority. The scales must be perfectly balanced;
any depiction showing them tilted is considered blasphemous.

His sacred days are the **first day of each season**, marking the
orderly transitions of the natural year. On these days, oaths are
traditionally sworn, contracts signed, and legal matters formalized.
Courts often schedule important verdicts for these dates.

**How He Is Worshipped**

Thandros worship centers on courthouse-temples where legal matters and
religious observances intertwine. Trials are conducted as religious
ceremonies, with priests of Thandros serving as judges or advisors to
secular magistrates. The architecture features clean lines, symmetrical
designs, and prominent displays of written law.

Worship services follow strict liturgies with no room for improvisation.
Worshippers recite codes of conduct, renew oaths of citizenship or
professional duty, and submit disputes for divine arbitration. The
faithful are expected to memorize legal codes relevant to their station.

Oath-swearing rituals are central to the faith. Marriage vows, business
contracts, military commissions, and governmental appointments all
traditionally invoke Thandros. Breaking an oath sworn before him is not
merely illegal but spiritually damaging.

**Major Temples and Sacred Sites**

The greatest temple of Thandros is the **High Court of Divine Law** in
Kaer Thandros, which serves as both the kingdom's supreme court and the
faith's holiest site. The building's architecture embodies Thandros'
principles: perfectly symmetrical, built to exacting specifications,
with every stone cut to precise measurements.

Other significant temples include the **Hall of Contracts** in Goldreach
(the oldest continuously operating courthouse in Thaldros), the
**Citadel of Oaths** in Ironhold, and numerous smaller
courthouse-temples throughout Thaldros.

**Historical Role**

The western continent bears Thandros' name---Thaldros---testament to his
influence on that empire's founding. When the first kingdoms formed
after the Worldrend, followers of Thandros provided the legal
frameworks, administrative systems, and governmental structures that
enabled civilization to rebuild.

Thandros worship was instrumental in ending the chaos of the Age of
Strife. His priests established the first post-Worldrend legal codes,
created courts to resolve disputes without violence, and developed the
systems of record-keeping that allowed complex society to function.

**Relationship to Other Gods**

Thandros stands in direct philosophical opposition to **Aethor**. Where
Thandros values order, Aethor champions freedom. This tension mirrors
the political divide between Thaldros and Aethoria and creates genuine
conflict between their followers. Despite this opposition, Thandros and
Aethor are not enemies---they

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

represent necessary poles of existence,
and most theologians believe the world requires both.

Thandros works closely with **Mordain**, who shares his lawful nature.
Both gods value judgment, proper procedure, and the enforcement of
cosmic rules. Their priesthoods often cooperate.

He respects **Moira** as the keeper of fate but sometimes chafes at
prophecies that seem to undermine the importance of law and choice.

His relationship with **Kael** is strained---the Wanderer's love of
trickery and situational ethics offends Thandros' preference for clear
rules and consistent application.

### 13.3 Aethor, The Liberator

![13.3 Aethor, The Liberator](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/god-aethor-liberation.jpg){width:325px}


**Full Name and Titles:** Aethor the Liberator, Lightbringer, Breaker of
Chains, The Dawn Lord, Champion of the Oppressed

**Sphere of Influence:** Freedom, Light, Hope, Revolution, Liberation,
Personal Choice

**Personality and Values**

Aethor stands in philosophical opposition to Thandros---where the
Lawbringer values order, the Liberator champions freedom. His followers
believe that tyranny is the greatest evil, that every being has the
right to determine their own destiny, and that hope must never be
extinguished no matter how dark the circumstances.

Aethor values courage, especially the courage to stand against injustice
when doing so brings personal risk. He admires those who sacrifice
comfort and safety for principles. He despises slavery, oppression, and
any system that treats people as property or denies them agency over
their own lives.

His faith teaches that light---both literal and metaphorical---reveals
truth and drives away the shadows where oppression hides. Transparency,
openness, and honesty are virtues; secrecy, manipulation, and deception
are tools of tyrants.

**Symbol and Holy Days**

His symbol is a **broken chain wreathed in sunlight**---the chain
representing bondage overcome, the sunlight representing the hope and
freedom that follow liberation.

His sacred day is the **Summer Solstice**, the longest day and the time
of greatest light. This festival celebrates freedom in all its forms,
commemorates historical liberations, and renews commitment to fighting
oppression. In Aethoria, the Summer Solstice is a major civic holiday
featuring public celebrations, historical reenactments, and the formal
freeing of any enslaved persons who have made their way to Aethorian
territory.

**How He Is Worshipped**

Aethor's temples are typically **open-air structures** designed to
welcome sunlight. Where enclosed buildings are necessary, they feature
large windows, skylights, and reflective surfaces to maximize natural
illumination. The faith holds that worship should occur under open sky
whenever possible.

Services are held at **sunrise**, when light returns to the world. These
dawn services feature hymns celebrating freedom, readings from the
Liberation Texts (accounts of historical struggles against oppression),
and communal affirmations of the faith's core principles.

The **liberation of the enslaved** is considered the highest form of
worship. Followers who free captives, shelter escaped slaves, or work to
dismantle systems of bondage are believed to earn Aethor's direct
blessing. Some temples maintain formal networks for helping escaped
slaves reach safety.

**Major Temples and Sacred Sites**

The holiest site is the **Temple of First Light** in Aethermere, built
on the spot where (according to tradition) the first slaves freed after
the Worldrend reached safety. The temple features the **Eternal
Dawn**---a magical effect that ensures sunlight illuminates the central
sanctuary regardless of time or weather.

Other significant temples include the **Lighthouse of Hope** on the
Drifting Chain (which guides ships and serves as a sanctuary for escaped
slaves), the **Hall of Broken Chains** in Crystalbrook, and numerous
smaller temples throughout Aethoria.

**Historical Role**

The eastern continent's name---Aethoria---echoes Aethor's influence.
When the continents separated in the Worldrend, survivors in the east
chose to build a

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

society based on freedom rather than hierarchy. Aethor
worship provided the philosophical foundation for the councils, the
rejection of hereditary aristocracy, and the commitment to personal
liberty that define Aethorian culture.

Aethor's faith was instrumental in the **Liberation of Aethoria**
(approximately 200 years before present), when Aethorian territories
that had fallen under Thaldros occupation successfully fought for
independence. This event is celebrated as the founding of free Aethoria.

**Relationship to Other Gods**

Aethor's opposition to **Thandros** defines much of his faith.
Followers of the Liberator see Thandros worship as providing cover for
tyranny---after all, oppressive regimes often justify themselves through
law and order. This theological conflict maps directly onto the
political tensions between Thaldros and Aethoria.

Aethor shares values with **Sylvara**, whose wild nature resists all
attempts at control. Their faiths cooperate frequently, with druids and
freedom fighters finding common cause against civilizations that would
tame both people and nature.

He respects **Sera's** compassion but sometimes conflicts with her
pacifist followers, who may prioritize peace over justice. Aethor's
faith teaches that some conflicts are necessary and righteous.

His relationship with **Kael** is generally positive---both gods value
individual freedom and distrust excessive authority. However, Aethor's
earnest idealism can clash with Kael's more pragmatic approach.

### 13.4 Moira, The Weaver

**Full Name and Titles:** Moira the Weaver, Keeper of Fate, The Oracle,
Lady of Threads, Guardian of Knowledge, The Three-Faced One

**Sphere of Influence:** Fate, Knowledge, Magic, Prophecy, Time, Secrets

**Personality and Values**

Moira sees the threads of fate that bind all things---past, present, and
future woven together in a tapestry of incomprehensible complexity. She
grants visions to her faithful but never reveals the full pattern,
believing that mortals must find their own way through the weave.

Her faith teaches that fate is woven but not immutable. The threads can
be followed in many directions; nothing is truly predetermined until it
occurs. This paradox lies at the heart of her teachings: fate exists and
can be perceived, but choice also exists and can change what was
foreseen.

Moira values knowledge above all---the seeking of it, the preservation
of it, and the wisdom to use it properly. She despises the destruction
of knowledge, whether through book-burning, the murder of scholars, or
the suppression of uncomfortable truths. Her temples serve as libraries
and archives as much as places of worship.

She is portrayed as patient, mysterious, and occasionally cryptic. She
rarely provides clear answers, preferring to guide questioners toward
their own understanding. Her prophecies are famous for coming true in
unexpected ways.

![13.4 Moira, The Weaver](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/god-moira-weaver-fate.jpg){width:325px}

**Symbol and Holy Days**

Her symbol is a **spindle with three threads**---representing past,
present, and future. The threads are often depicted as silver, gold, and
black, symbolizing what was, what is, and what might be.

Her sacred day is the **Night of the Seven Stars**, a rare celestial
alignment when seven specific stars form a pattern visible only once
every few decades. During this night, divinations are believed to be
especially accurate, and the veil between present and future grows thin.
When the alignment is not occurring, she is honored on nights of meteor
showers and celestial phenomena.

**How She Is Worshipped**

Moira's temples function as **libraries, archives, and centers of
learning** as much as religious institutions. Her priests are scholars
first and clergy second. Worship often takes the form of study,
research, and the preservation of knowledge.

**Divination rituals** are central to her faith. Worshippers seek
guidance through various methods: reading the stars, interpreting
dreams, casting runes, or entering meditative trances. The accuracy of
these divinations varies---Moira reveals what she chooses to reveal, and
her reasons are her own.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

The faith maintains **extensive archives** of prophecy, attempting to
correlate predictions with eventual outcomes. These records span
centuries and represent one of the most valuable historical resources in
Tirvandor.

Ceremonies often occur during celestial events---eclipses, meteor
showers, planetary alignments. The faith maintains sophisticated
astronomical knowledge to predict these occasions.

**Major Temples and Sacred Sites**

The greatest temple is the **Starfall Observatory** in the city of
Starfall, where House Starweaver serves as hereditary priests. This
complex combines religious functions with astronomical observation,
maintaining records of celestial movements stretching back to before the
Worldrend.

The **Academies of Moira** in Silverpine and Aethermere function as both
temples and magical universities, training mages in the arcane arts
while instilling religious devotion. These institutions sometimes clash
with secular authorities over the role of magic in society.

The **Black Archive** beneath Silverpine Magical Academy is a sacred
site of a different sort---a repository of forbidden knowledge, texts
too dangerous for general access but too valuable to destroy.

**Historical Role**

Moira's worship played a crucial role in preserving knowledge through
the Worldrend and its aftermath. Her priests prioritized saving texts,
copying manuscripts, and maintaining oral traditions during the years of
chaos. Much of what is known about pre-Worldrend history survives
because her followers treated knowledge preservation as a sacred duty.

Her prophecies have shaped major historical events, though the exact
nature of this influence is debated. Did foreknowledge allow people to
change fate, or did the prophecies themselves cause the events they
predicted? Theologians have argued this question for centuries without
resolution.

**Relationship to Other Gods**

Moira maintains **cordial relationships with all the Seven**, seeing
herself as a recorder of their actions rather than a participant in
their conflicts. She claims neutrality in the disputes between other
gods, though some theologians note that her prophecies often seem to
favor certain outcomes.

She works closely with **Mordain**, whose domain of Memory overlaps with
her concern for preserving the past. Their priesthoods often cooperate
on historical matters.

Her relationship with **Thandros** is complex---he values the order that
comes from knowing the future, but also values free will, which prophecy
seems to undermine. Their theological debates continue across centuries.

**Sylvara** represents her opposite in some ways---wild nature versus
studied knowledge, intuition versus analysis. Yet Moira respects the
wild goddess' understanding of cycles and patterns in nature.

### 13.5 Kael, The Wanderer

![13.5 Kael, The Wanderer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/god-kael-wanderer.jpg){width:325px}


**Full Name and Titles:** Kael the Wanderer, Lord of Roads, The Lucky
One, Master of the Crossroads, The Clever God, Patron of Travelers

**Sphere of Influence:** Travel, Trade, Luck, Trickery, Crossroads,
Commerce, Cleverness

**Personality and Values**

Kael is the patron of travelers, merchants, and anyone who lives by
their wits. He values cleverness over brute force and believes the
journey matters more than the destination. His followers learn that
adaptability, quick thinking, and a willingness to take calculated risks
are the keys to success.

His faith teaches that fortune favors the bold and the clever. Those who
take no chances receive no rewards; those who adapt to circumstances
rather than fighting them succeed where others fail. He has no patience
for rigidity or those who follow rules for rules' sake.

Kael is often depicted as a trickster, delighting in clever deceptions
and unexpected reversals. However, his faith distinguishes between
clever tricks that harm no innocents and malicious deception that causes
suffering. The former earns his approval; the latter does not.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

He particularly values merchants and traders, seeing commerce as a form
of connection that binds distant peoples together. Fair dealing is
important---not because of abstract principles, but because merchants
who cheat their customers eventually run out of customers.

**Symbol and Holy Days**

His symbol is a **compass rose with a winding road**---representing both
the many directions one might travel and the twisting path that actual
journeys follow.

His sacred day is the **First Day of Spring**, marking the beginning of
the traditional travel season when roads become passable and trading
caravans begin their journeys. This festival features celebrations of
successful journeys, offerings for safe travels ahead, and the
traditional exchange of travelers' tales.

**How He Is Worshipped**

Kael worship is **decentralized and informal**. Rather than great
temples, his faith maintains countless **roadside shrines** at
crossroads, mountain passes, and harbor approaches. Travelers leave
small offerings---coins, food, tokens of their journey---in exchange for
blessings of safe passage.

**Blessing ceremonies** for caravans, ships, and individual travelers
are common before any significant journey. These typically involve
prayers for favorable conditions, protection from hazards, and good
fortune in the ventures ahead.

His priests are **wanderers themselves**, rarely remaining in one place
for long. They travel the roads offering spiritual guidance, practical
advice, and sometimes serving as intermediaries in disputes between
merchants. Many are also skilled healers, understanding that travelers
far from home often need medical assistance.

Gambling, games of chance, and contests of wit are considered forms of
worship when conducted in good faith. The faith sees luck as a divine
gift and the ability to recognize and seize opportunities as a spiritual
skill.

**Major Temples and Sacred Sites**

The largest temple is the **Hall of Ten Thousand Roads** in Goldreach, a
vast complex that serves as a gathering place for merchants, a
repository of maps and travel information, and a center for settling
commercial disputes. The architecture features numerous entrances and
exits, emphasizing that there are always multiple paths forward.

**Port Myrthen** hosts the **Temple of Favorable Winds**, important to
sailors throughout the Sundering Sea.

The most sacred sites, however, are the **ancient crossroads** scattered
throughout both continents---places where major trade routes have
intersected since before the Worldrend. These locations are marked by
standing stones, weathered statues, or simple cairns, maintained by
local followers regardless of political boundaries.

**Historical Role**

Kael worship facilitated the rebuilding of trade networks after the
Worldrend. When commerce collapsed, his followers were among the first
to venture across dangerous roads and uncharted waters to reestablish
connections between isolated communities. The faith's emphasis on fair
dealing helped create trust in an era of chaos.

The modern Merchant League traces its origins to alliances formed among
Kael-worshipping merchants in the early post-Worldrend centuries. His
influence on commercial law and trading customs persists throughout
Tirvandor.

**Relationship to Other Gods**

Kael's relationship with **Thandros** is strained. The Wanderer's love
of situational ethics and clever tricks offends the Lawbringer's
preference for clear rules and consistent application. Their followers
frequently clash over questions of commerce, contracts, and what
constitutes fair dealing.

He gets along well with **Aethor**, sharing appreciation for individual
freedom and distrust of excessive authority. However, Kael's pragmatism
can conflict with Aethor's idealism.

His relationship with **Sera** is warm---both gods value those who help
strangers, and travelers often depend on the kindness of healers in
unfamiliar places.

He respects **Moira's** knowledge but finds her cryptic pronouncements
frustrating. Kael prefers to make his own luck rather than rely on fate.

### 13.6 Sera, The Healer

![13.6 Sera, The Healer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/god-sera-the-healer.jpg){width:325px}

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

**Full Name and Titles:** Sera the Healer, Lady of Mercy, The
Compassionate One, Mother of Restoration, Guardian of the Suffering

**Sphere of Influence:** Life, Healing, Mercy, Compassion, Birth,
Comfort

**Personality and Values**

Sera is the most universally beloved of the Seven Ascended. Her temples
serve as hospitals, her clergy as healers, and her teaching that all
life is sacred resonates across cultural and political boundaries. She
represents compassion in its purest form---help for those in need
without expectation of reward or judgment of worthiness.

Her faith teaches that mercy is strength, not weakness. It takes courage
to show compassion when anger would be easier, to heal an enemy, to
comfort the dying even when nothing more can be done. The greatest acts
of mercy are those that cost the giver something.

Sera values life above all other concerns. Her priests heal soldiers
regardless of which army they fight for, treat criminals alongside
victims, and shelter the persecuted without asking what they flee. This
stance sometimes brings them into conflict with secular authorities who
see such neutrality as dangerous.

She is portrayed as gentle but not passive, kind but not naive. Her
followers understand that protecting life sometimes requires difficult
choices, including the choice to fight against those who would destroy
it.

**Symbol and Holy Days**

Her symbol is a **golden chalice overflowing with water**---representing
healing that flows abundantly to all who need it, without limit or
restriction.

Her sacred day is the **Spring Equinox**, when life returns to the world
after winter's death. This festival celebrates birth, renewal, and the
triumph of life over darkness. New children are traditionally blessed,
convalescents give thanks for recovery, and communities honor those who
provided healing throughout the year.

**How She Is Worshipped**

Sera's temples function primarily as **hospitals and hospices**.
Worship and healing occur simultaneously; to care for the sick is to
honor her. The architecture emphasizes cleanliness, light, and comfort
for patients rather than impressive displays of religious authority.

**Healing the sick** is considered the highest form of devotion. Priests
spend most of their time providing medical care, and religious services
are often conducted in wards where patients can participate from their
beds. Donations to the temple fund care for those who cannot pay.

**Comfort of the dying** is equally important. When healing is
impossible, Sera's followers provide what comfort they can---physical
ease, emotional support, and spiritual preparation for what lies beyond.
The faith teaches that death itself is not an enemy, only unnecessary
suffering.

Midwifery is a sacred calling, and most births in Tirvandor are attended
by Sera's followers. The protection of mothers and infants is a
religious duty taken very seriously.

**Major Temples and Sacred Sites**

Every major city has a **Temple of Sera** serving as its primary
hospital. The largest is the **House of Endless Mercy** in Aethermere,
which can accommodate over a thousand patients and trains healers who
serve throughout both continents.

The **Spring of Restoration** near Silverpine is a sacred site where
natural springs are believed to have healing properties. Pilgrims travel
great distances to bathe in its waters, and the surrounding temple
complex provides both physical care and spiritual guidance.

**Historical Role**

During the years of plague and chaos following the Worldrend, Sera's
followers were essential to survival. While others fled from disease,
her priests walked toward it, caring for the sick even when it cost them
their own lives. This sacrifice earned the faith deep respect that
persists to the present day.

The modern practice of medicine in Tirvandor owes much to her followers,
who developed treatment protocols, trained healers, and established the
principle that care should be available to all regardless of ability to
pay.

**Relationship to Other Gods**

Sera maintains **friendly relationships with all the Seven**, believing
that healing should transcend other conflicts. Her temples provide
sanctuary to followers of all gods, and her priests refuse to take sides
in theological disputes.

She works closely with **Mordain**, whose domain of death might seem
opposed but actually complements hers. His followers ease the passing of
those she cannot save, and both faiths cooperate on questions of what
happens after death.

Her relationship with **Aethor** is warm but occasionally complicated.
She shares his compassion but sometimes disagrees with his followers'
willingness to cause harm in pursuit of justice. Some wars might be
necessary, but all wars create suffering she must heal.

She has the most distant relationship with **Thandros**, whose law can
require punishment she finds harsh. However, she does not actively
oppose him, understanding that order and healing both serve the common
good.

### 13.7 Mordain, The Sentinel

**Full Name and Titles:** Mordain the Sentinel, Guardian of the Dead,
The Judge of Souls, Lord of Memory, The Eternal Watcher, Enemy of the
Undead

**Sphere of Influence:** Death, Protection, Judgment, Memory, the
Afterlife, Opposition to Undeath

**Personality and Values**

Mordain guides souls to their proper rest and stands eternal guard
against those who would disturb the dead. He is not evil---he is
necessary. Death is natural, part of

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

the cycle that makes room for new
life, and Mordain ensures that cycle continues properly.

His faith teaches that death should not be feared but accepted as the
natural conclusion of mortal existence. The dead deserve honor and rest;
disturbing their remains or trapping their souls is blasphemy. Most
significantly, undeath---the state of being neither alive nor truly
dead---is the greatest abomination against the natural order.

Mordain values memory, the preservation of what the dead accomplished
during their lives. His temples maintain records of the departed,
ensuring that lives are not forgotten even as bodies return to dust.
This concern for memory makes his faith important for historical
preservation.

He is portrayed as solemn, fair, and absolutely implacable. Every soul
eventually comes before him; every life eventually ends. He cannot be
bargained with, bribed, or deceived. But he is not cruel---he judges
fairly and dispatches souls to the destinations they have earned through
their choices.

![13.7 Mordain, The Sentinel](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/god-mordain-sentinel-death.jpg){width:325px}

**Symbol and Holy Days**

His symbol is a **shield bearing a closed eye**---representing both
protection (the shield) and the eternal rest of death (the closed eye).
Some variants show the eye slightly open, suggesting vigilance against
those who would disturb the dead.

His sacred day is the **Autumn Equinox**, when the world begins to die
back toward winter. This festival commemorates the dead, honors
ancestors, and includes rituals to ensure proper rest for those who have
passed. Graves are tended, memories are shared, and offerings are made
to ease souls' passage.

**How He Is Worshipped**

Mordain's temples are typically located **near graveyards and cremation
sites**, serving as the interface between the living and the dead. The
architecture is austere and dignified, designed to inspire reflection
rather than fear.

**Funeral rites** are central to the faith. Mordain's priests conduct
services that ease souls' passage to the afterlife, comfort the
bereaved, and ensure proper treatment of remains. The specific practices
vary by culture---burial, cremation, sky burial, or sea burial are all
acceptable if performed with proper respect.

**Memorial services** maintain connections with the departed. The faith
keeps records of the dead and their deeds, ensuring that ancestors are
not forgotten. Families regularly visit temples to honor their dead and
add their stories to the archives.

The **destruction of undead** is considered a sacred duty. Mordain's
followers are trained to recognize and combat vampires, liches, ghosts,
and other undead creatures. This aspect of the faith creates
warrior-priests comparable to paladins of other gods.

**Major Temples and Sacred Sites**

Major temples are found near major graveyards throughout Tirvandor. The
**Hall of Final Rest** in Kaer Thandros maintains records of every
documented death in the kingdom's history---millions of entries dating
back over a thousand years.

The **Valley of Bones** in the Contested Lands is a sacred site where
battles during the Age of Strife left so many dead that the valley floor
is still littered with remains. Mordain's followers maintain a temple
there, ensuring proper rest for fallen warriors and preventing
necromantic exploitation.

**Historical Role**

After the Worldrend killed millions, Mordain's followers faced an
overwhelming task: ensuring proper rest for the countless dead while
preventing the rise of undead hordes that could have overwhelmed the
survivors. Their success in this effort prevented a secondary
catastrophe and earned the faith enduring respect.

The modern practice of recording deaths, maintaining genealogies, and
properly disposing of remains derives largely from traditions
established by Mordain's followers during the recovery period.

**Relationship to Other Gods**

Mordain works closely with **Thandros**, sharing his lawful nature and
respect for proper procedure. Both gods value judgment, cosmic rules,
and appropriate consequences. Their priesthoods often cooperate on
matters of justice.

His relationship with **Sera** is complementary---she preserves life as
long as possible; he ensures dignity and rest when life ends. They
represent two aspects of

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

caring for mortal beings, and their priests frequently work together.

He opposes **Kael's** more chaotic followers who might see death as
just another obstacle to overcome through cleverness. The two gods are
not enemies, but their approaches to cosmic order differ significantly.

His relationship with **Moira** is collegial---both serve as keepers of
what has passed, she through knowledge and he through memory. They share
an interest in historical preservation.

### 13.8 Sylvara, The Wild

![13.8 Sylvara, The Wild](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/god-sylvara-nature-wild.jpg){width:325px}


**Full Name and Titles:** Sylvara the Wild, Lady of Storms, Mother of
Beasts, The Green Goddess, Voice of the World, The Untamed One

**Sphere of Influence:** Nature, Growth, Storms, Beasts, Seasons, the
Primal World

**Personality and Values**

Sylvara embodies the natural world in all its beauty and brutality. She
represents the cycle of life, death, and rebirth---the storm that
destroys and the rain that nourishes. Her worship predates written
history, and some believe she is not a god at all but the world itself
given voice.

Her faith teaches that nature must maintain balance. Predators cull the
weak; decay feeds new growth; storms clear deadwood for fresh
beginnings. This cycle should not be interfered with, though it can be
worked alongside. Civilizations that respect nature can coexist with
wilderness; those that seek to dominate or destroy it invite
catastrophe.

Sylvara is neither good nor evil by mortal standards. She values
strength and adaptation---those who survive demonstrate fitness to
continue. But she also values protection---the strong defending the weak
until the weak become strong themselves. The wolf that guards her pups
and the mother bear defending her cubs both demonstrate her principles.

She is portrayed as wild, unpredictable, and fundamentally
incomprehensible to those who live entirely in civilization. Her moods
shift like weather; her blessings are as likely to challenge as comfort;
her followers accept that nature does not conform to mortal wishes.

**Symbol and Holy Days**

Her symbol is an **oak tree struck by lightning, still
growing**---representing resilience, the creative power of destruction,
and the continuation of life through apparent catastrophe.

She is honored on **both Equinoxes**, the balance points of the year.
The Spring Equinox celebrates renewal and growth; the Autumn Equinox
acknowledges death and preparation for winter. Both festivals involve
ceremonies in natural settings, offerings returned to the wild, and
celebrations of seasonal transitions.

**How She Is Worshipped**

Sylvara's temples are **sacred groves, stone circles, and natural
places** rather than constructed buildings. Where structures exist, they
incorporate living plants, open to sky and weather, designed to blur the
boundary between civilization and wilderness.

Her primary clergy are **druids** rather than traditional priests. These
servants of nature learn to work with ley lines, shapeshift into animal
forms, and command the forces of weather and growth. Their training
takes place in the wilderness, far from cities, and may last decades.

**Seasonal ceremonies** mark transitions in the natural year. Planting
festivals, harvest celebrations, and rituals acknowledging the coming of
winter all fall under her purview. Farmers who work the land are among
her most common worshippers, understanding that their prosperity depends
on nature's cooperation.

**Animal offerings** (releasing captured creatures, protecting
endangered species, culling invasive ones) are considered proper
worship. Her followers also practice **rewilding**, allowing cultivated
areas to return to wilderness as offering.

**Major Temples and Sacred Sites**

The **Emerald Deeps** of Aethoria contain her most sacred groves, places
where the forest has remained uncut since before the Worldrend. Druids
maintain these sites, and entering them uninvited is considered both
trespass and blasphemy.

The **Wildgrove** is another major sacred site, home to an order of
druids who serve as her primary clergy in western Thaldros.

The **Storm Peaks** of the Ironspine Mountains host shrines to her storm
aspect, maintained by priests who

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

study weather patterns and seek to understand her most destructive moods.

**Historical Role**

Sylvara worship predates the other Ascended, potentially dating to
before the Worldrend or even before human civilization. Her druids
maintained knowledge of natural cycles through the chaos that followed
the cataclysm, understanding which plants were edible, which herbs had
healing properties, and how to survive in wilderness.

Her influence helped prevent the total devastation of Tirvandor's
ecosystems after the Worldrend. While much was destroyed, her followers
worked to restore balance, protect endangered species, and ensure that
nature could recover.

**Relationship to Other Gods**

Sylvara represents the **wild opposite of Thandros'** ordered
civilization. Their followers often clash over questions of development,
urbanization, and the proper relationship between settled peoples and
wild lands. However, most theologians see this as a necessary tension
rather than true enmity.

She shares common ground with **Aethor**, whose love of freedom
resonates with her untamed nature. Their followers often cooperate
against civilizations that would control both people and nature.

Her relationship with **Sera** is complex---both value life, but Sylvara
accepts death as natural where Sera fights against it. Sylvara's storms
kill; Sera's healers save. Yet both serve the continuation of life in
their own ways.

**Moira's** ordered knowledge of fate contrasts with Sylvara's wild
unpredictability. They represent different ways of understanding the
world---through study and through experience, through pattern-seeking
and through acceptance of chaos.

### 13.9 Relationships Between the Seven


The Seven Ascended are not a unified pantheon but seven distinct beings
with their own personalities, goals, and conflicts. Their relationships
shape both divine and mortal politics throughout Tirvandor.

**The Fundamental Opposition: Thandros and Aethor**

The tension between the Lawbringer and the Liberator represents the
central theological conflict of Tirvandor. Order versus freedom, law
versus liberty, structure versus spontaneity---these opposing principles
manifest in everything from individual moral choices to the cold war
between continents.

Most theologians believe this opposition is necessary and even healthy.
A world of pure order would stagnate; a world of pure freedom would
collapse into chaos. The tension between these principles creates space
for growth, change, and meaningful choice.

\column

**The Alliance of Duty: Thandros and Mordain**

The two lawful gods share values and frequently cooperate. Both believe
in proper procedure, cosmic rules, and appropriate consequences for
actions. Their priesthoods work together on matters of justice, with
Mordain's concern for final judgment complementing Thandros' focus on
mortal law.

**The Partnership of Care: Sera and Mordain**

The goddess of life and the god of death might seem opposed, but they
represent complementary aspects of caring for mortal beings. Sera
preserves life; Mordain ensures dignity in death. Together, they address
the full span of mortal existence. Their priests often work side by
side, healers and grave wardens cooperating on the transition from life
to death.

**The Freedom Alliance: Aethor and Sylvara**

Both gods value freedom from constraint---Aethor for people, Sylvara for
nature. Their followers often find common cause against civilizations
that would control both. The druid circles and the liberation movements
have cooperated historically on issues affecting both populations and
ecosystems.

**The Neutral Observer: Moira**

The Weaver maintains cordial relationships with all the Seven,
positioning herself as recorder and observer rather than participant in
their conflicts. Her prophecies affect all equally, and her followers
claim neutrality in divine politics. However, some theologians note that
her cryptic pronouncements often seem to influence outcomes in
particular directions.

**The Wild Card: Kael**

The Wanderer resists easy categorization. He values freedom (like
Aethor) but also pragmatism (unlike Aethor's idealism). He dislikes
rigid rules (opposing Thandros) but also appreciates the order that
makes trade possible (somewhat agreeing with Thandros). His position
shifts depending on circumstances, which his followers see as wisdom and
his critics see as inconsistency.

**The Celestial Council**

Established in 400 CR, the Celestial Council provides a forum for
coordination among the major religious institutions. Representatives of
all Seven meet periodically to discuss matters of common
concern---responding to threats against the faithful, coordinating
relief efforts during disasters, and maintaining some semblance of
inter-faith cooperation.

The Council has no enforcement power but significant moral authority.
Its decisions influence how ordinary worshippers view inter-faith
relations, and its pronouncements carry weight with secular authorities
who must balance multiple religious interests.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 13: The Seven Ascended}}
\page

![Chapter 14: The Primordials](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/world/tirvandor-world-ancient-precursor-ruins.jpg){position:absolute,top:0,left:0,width:100%,height:340px}

{{margin-top:290px}}

## Chapter 14: The Primordials


### 14.1 Nature of the Primordials


The Primordials are not gods in the traditional sense but elemental
forces that predate the current pantheon. Ancient texts suggest they
existed before the Seven Ascended, before the mortal races, perhaps
before creation itself took its current form. They are worshipped not
through temples but through primal magic and druidic rites.

The relationship between Primordials and gods remains unclear. Some
scholars believe the gods emerged from the Primordials---that the Seven
Ascended drew their original power from these elemental forces before
transcending to true divinity. Others argue that Primordials and gods
represent fundamentally different categories of existence, coexisting in
ways mortals cannot fully comprehend.

Unlike the Seven Ascended, Primordials do not have personalities in the
mortal sense. They do not make moral judgments, answer prayers, or take
sides in conflicts. They simply *are*---vast, impersonal forces that
shape reality through their existence rather than their will.

### 14.2 The Six Known Primordials


**Ignar, the First Flame**

The Primordial of Fire embodies creation and destruction through flame.
Ignar represents the spark that ignites change, the forge-fire that
transforms raw material into crafted works, and the wildfire that clears
away the old to make room for the new.

Current theories suggest Ignar sleeps beneath volcanic regions, its
presence causing the geothermal activity that characterizes the Ashfall
Wastes and similar locations. The fire cults of Ashgate maintain that
their city exists because Ignar tolerates it---that the

\column
{{margin-top:290px}}

volcano's eruptions are contained by the Primordial's slumbering will.

Druids who attune to Ignar's power can command flames and resist fire,
but they also tend toward passionate temperaments and difficulty with
patience. The element demands expression.

**Thalassia, the Endless Depth**

The Primordial of Water embodies the primal ocean from which all life
emerged. Thalassia represents the depths that hold secrets, the currents
that connect distant shores, and the overwhelming power of storm and
tide.

Thalassia is believed to be aware but distant, its consciousness
embodied in the Sundering Sea itself. Some sailors claim to have
glimpsed its attention during storms---a vast awareness that notices
mortal ships the way a human might notice an ant on their arm. Whether
it cares about mortals at all remains debated.

The Sundering Sea's unpredictable nature, its strange currents, and the
phenomena sailors report may all be manifestations of Thalassia's
dreaming presence.

**Terrax, the Stone That Dreams**

The Primordial of Earth embodies the bones of the world---eternal,
patient, and fundamentally stable. Terrax represents permanence,
endurance, and the slow processes that shape landscapes over millennia.

Terrax is ever-present in the deep places beneath Tirvandor. Dwarven
legends speak of encountering its awareness in the deepest delves---not
as a being but as a pervasive sense that the stone itself is alive and
watching. Whether this represents true consciousness or merely the
attribution of intent to natural phenomena, none can say.

Those who attune to Terrax's power find themselves becoming more
patient, more enduring, and sometimes more rigid in their thinking. The
earth does not change quickly, and neither do those who become too
closely bound to it.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 14: The Primordials}}
\page

**Zephyros, the Breath of Freedom**

The Primordial of Air embodies wind, sky, and the space between things.
Zephyros represents freedom of movement, the carrying of messages across
vast distances, and the invisible force that shapes weather and climate.

Unlike the other Primordials, Zephyros cannot be localized. It is
constantly moving, never contained, present wherever air flows. This
makes it perhaps the most accessible Primordial to mortal
perception---every breath taken is an interaction with Zephyros' domain.

Those who attune to air magic often become restless, uncomfortable with
confinement, and possessed of wanderlust that can never be fully
satisfied.

**Verdania, the Ever-Growing**

The Primordial of Life (sometimes called Wood or Growth) embodies the
force of living things---the drive to survive, reproduce, and spread.
Verdania represents the cycle of growth and decay, the competition for
resources, and the overwhelming fecundity of nature.

Verdania is present in every growing thing, from the smallest moss to
the largest forest. Sacred groves are places where its presence
concentrates, where the life force flows more strongly than elsewhere.
The Emerald Deeps of Aethoria are considered one of the greatest
concentrations of Verdania's power in Tirvandor.

Those who attune to life magic often find themselves becoming more
vital, more connected to natural cycles, and sometimes troubled by the
artificial constraints of civilization.

**Noctis, the Void Between**

The Primordial of Darkness (sometimes called Shadow or Void) embodies
the spaces between existence---potential unrealized, secrets hidden, and
the mystery of what lies beyond the known. Noctis represents not evil
but absence, not malice but mystery.

Noctis lurks in shadows, neither good nor evil but simply *other*. It is
the Primordial most difficult to understand because understanding
requires illumination, and Noctis is the absence of light. Some scholars
believe it represents possibility---the infinite potential of what has
not yet been determined.

Those who attune to shadow magic must be careful not to lose themselves
in the darkness. The void between offers power but demands that its
wielders maintain their sense of self against the pull of dissolution.

### 14.3 Primordial Influence Today


The Primordials influence the modern world in several ways:

**Primal Magic**

Druids and certain other practitioners draw power directly from the
Primordials rather than from the gods. This magic tends to be less
refined than divine magic---rawer, more powerful, and more dangerous. A
cleric channels their deity's will; a druid channels elemental force
that has no will to channel.

The Green Faith regulates who may learn primal magic, ensuring that
practitioners understand both its power and its dangers. Uncontrolled
primal magic can cause environmental catastrophes.

**Sacred Sites**

Locations where Primordial presence concentrates are sacred to druids
and often avoided by others. These include volcanic regions (Ignar),
deep ocean trenches (Thalassia), ancient mountain caverns (Terrax), high
peaks and windy places (Zephyros), old-growth forests (Verdania), and
lightless caves (Noctis).

**Environmental Effects**

The Primordials' presence shapes the natural world. Unusual weather
patterns, strange geological formations, unexplained fertility in
certain regions, and areas of perpetual darkness may all result from
Primordial influence.

### 14.4 Primordial Cults


While the Primordials are not gods in the traditional sense, some
mortals worship them anyway. These cults range from benign
nature-reverence to dangerous extremism.

**Legitimate Practices**

Druids honor the Primordials through rituals that acknowledge their
power without expecting reciprocal attention. These practices focus on
maintaining balance between elemental forces and protecting natural
sites where Primordial presence concentrates.

**Fire Cults**

The most controversial Primordial worship centers on Ignar. Fire cults
operate openly in Ashgate, where volcanic activity makes fire-worship
culturally acceptable, but are suppressed in most other regions due to
their tendency toward destructive rituals.

Some fire cultists genuinely seek to honor the creative aspect of
flame---the forge-fire and hearth-fire. Others are drawn to destruction,
believing that burning away the corrupt world will allow something
better to emerge.

**Dangerous Extremes**

The Bound Ancients imprisoned beneath Tirvandor may include corrupted
aspects of Primordial power. Some cults worship these entities,
believing that freeing them will restore the world to its primal state.
These cults are actively dangerous and hunted by most civilized
authorities.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 14: The Primordials}}
\page

## Chapter 15: Regional Powers and the Forgotten Ones


### 15.1 Regional Deities


Beyond the Seven Ascended, numerous deities are worshipped in specific
regions or by particular cultures. These gods lack the universal reach
of the Seven but may be the primary deities in their territories.

**Thaldros Regional Powers**

*Korak the Ironbound*

The god of War, Strength, and Honor in Battle is venerated throughout
the military centers of Thaldros. His symbol is a sword crossing an axe,
and his alignment is Lawful Neutral. Soldiers, mercenaries, and warriors
honor him before battle and credit him with victories.

His teachings emphasize that strength protects the weak, that honor in
combat matters as much as victory, and that discipline wins wars. Major
temples exist in Ironhold and military fortresses throughout Thaldros.

*Lyssandra the Hearthkeeper*

The goddess of Home, Family, Peace, and Agriculture is worshipped
primarily in rural areas of Thaldros. Her symbol is a hearth fire, and
her alignment is Neutral Good. Farmers, parents, and community leaders
invoke her protection.

Her teachings hold that a strong home is the foundation of society and
that family should be protected above all. She represents the peaceful
side of Thaldros culture often overshadowed by military emphasis.

*Gorath the Forgemaster*

The god of Crafting, Mountains, Law, and Protection is dominant among
dwarves and strong among blacksmiths and craftspeople throughout
Thaldros. His symbol is an anvil with crossed hammers, and his alignment
is Lawful Neutral.

His teachings emphasize that quality work honors the divine and that an
oath once given is sacred. Dwarven communities maintain his most
elaborate temples, but any smith of quality likely keeps his shrine.

**Aethorian Regional Powers**

*Ealasaïd the Dreamweaver*

The goddess of Dreams, Illusion, Art, and Inspiration is worshipped by
artists, bards, and elven communities throughout Aethoria. Her symbol is
a butterfly made of moonlight, and her alignment is Chaotic Good.

Her teachings suggest that reality is what mortals dream it to be and
that art touches the divine. Her followers include painters, musicians,
poets, and those who seek visions through meditation or ritual.

*Vorath the Primal*

The god of Beasts, Hunt, Survival, and Strength is honored by rangers,
hunters, barbarians, and beast-folk tribes in the wild regions of
Aethoria. His symbol is a bear paw with claws extended, and his
alignment is Chaotic Neutral.

His teachings are simple: the strong survive, hunt with honor, and
respect the prey. He represents the untamed aspects of Aethorian
culture.

*Merenth the Lifegiver*

The goddess of Healing, Life, Growth, and Fertility serves as an
Aethorian counterpart to Sera, though with different emphasis. Her
symbol is a green leaf with a water drop, and her alignment is Neutral
Good.

Her teachings hold that life is sacred, healing is holy duty, and growth
should be nurtured. She is particularly popular in agricultural
communities and among midwives.

**Island and Sea Powers**

*Kalythra the Stormmother*

The goddess of Sea, Storms, Chaos, and Freedom is worshipped by sailors
and coastal communities throughout the Sundering Sea. Her symbol is a
crashing wave with a lightning bolt, and her alignment is Chaotic
Neutral.

Her teachings demand respect for the power of nature, adaptation rather
than resistance, and acceptance that the sea gives and takes as it
wills. Sailors make offerings before voyages and during storms.

*Tharivol the Many-Faced*

The god of Change, Luck, Trickery, and Adaptation is honored by
gamblers, pirates, adventurers, and those in transition. His symbol is
dice showing all different numbers simultaneously, and his alignment is
Chaotic Neutral.

His teachings embrace change as inevitable, hold that luck favors the
bold, and advise adaptation over rigid resistance. He is particularly
popular in Port Myrthen and among those who live by their wits.

### 15.2 The Forgotten Ones


These deities were once worshipped but their followings have faded or
been actively suppressed. They represent the dangerous, the heretical,
or the simply obsolete.

**Vorthane the Conqueror**

Once the god of Empire, Domination, and Tyranny, Vorthane commanded
significant worship during the Age of Tyrants when powerful individuals
ruled through force. His symbol was an iron fist, and his alignment was
Lawful Evil.

Worship of Vorthane was banned after his followers attempted to conquer
both continents through coordinated military and magical campaigns. The
resulting wars caused massive casualties before the cult was broken.

Secret cultists remain, drawn to his promise of power through
domination. They operate in shadows, sometimes infiltrating legitimate
power structures to advance their goals of conquest and control.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 15: Regional Powers and the Forgotten Ones}}
\page

**Shaelis the Whisperer**

Once the goddess of Secrets, Poison, and Assassination, Shaelis
represented the dark side of information---knowledge used to kill rather
than enlighten. Her symbol was a dagger in shadow, and her alignment was
Neutral Evil.

Worship of Shaelis has been suppressed by most governments, who
recognize the danger of organized assassination cults. However, small
cells still operate in shadows, offering services to those who need
enemies removed quietly.

Her remaining followers claim she represents necessary evil---that some
secrets must be kept, some poisons administered, some threats eliminated
before they can cause greater harm.

**Morthax the Ever-Dying**

Once the god of Undeath, Decay, and Entropy, Morthax offered an
alternative to Mordain's natural death---eternal existence through
undeath. His symbol was a skull with green flames, and his alignment was
Neutral Evil.

Mordain's clergy actively hunt Morthax worshippers, viewing undeath as
the greatest blasphemy against the natural order. Necromancers may
secretly serve Morthax, believing that death can be overcome through
sufficient will and power.

The conflict between Mordain and Morthax worshippers has lasted for
millennia and shows no signs of resolution.

**The Bound God**

The most mysterious of the Forgotten Ones, the Bound God's former
domains are unknown because records were deliberately destroyed. Its
symbol is unknown. Speaking its true name is taboo---forbidden not
merely by law but by divine decree from the other gods.

According to fragmentary accounts, the Bound God was imprisoned before
the Worldrend by the combined action of the other deities. What it did
to merit such punishment, what powers it once wielded, and whether it
might someday escape---these questions have no public answers.

Some scholars believe the Bound God may be connected to the Bound
Ancients imprisoned beneath Tirvandor. Others argue these are separate
entities entirely. The truth, if known at all, is known only to the gods
themselves.

## Chapter 16: Religious Structures and Faith


### 16.1 Major Religious Organizations


**The Celestial Council**

Established in 400 CR, the Celestial Council is a gathering of high
priests from all Seven Ascended that meets every seven years to discuss
matters affecting all faiths. It has no enforcement power but carries
significant moral authority.

The Council was founded in the aftermath of religious conflicts during
the Age of Recovery, when different faiths competed for followers among
the struggling survivors. Its purpose was to establish norms of
inter-faith conduct and prevent religious wars.

Representatives from each of the Seven discuss matters of common
concern: responding to threats against the faithful (such as undead
plagues or demonic incursions), coordinating relief efforts during
disasters, resolving territorial disputes between temples, and
maintaining basic inter-faith cooperation.

The Council's decisions are advisory rather than binding, but temples
that ignore Council pronouncements risk losing the cooperation of other
faiths---a significant penalty in a world where most people worship
multiple gods.

**The Order of the Threefold Path**

This order of paladins and clerics serves Aethor, Moira, and Mordain
together, believing these three gods form a complete cycle of light,
shadow, and ending. Members are elite monster hunters and protectors of
the innocent.

The philosophy holds that Aethor brings light that reveals truth, Moira
weaves the threads of fate that determine outcomes, and Mordain ensures
proper endings. Together, they represent the full span of
existence---birth through death, illumination through obscurity.

The Order specializes in hunting supernatural threats: undead, demons,
aberrations, and other beings that threaten the natural order. Their
members are famous for their effectiveness and their unusual theological
perspective.

**The Green Faith**

A druidic organization spanning both continents, the Green Faith is
dedicated to Sylvara and the Primordials. They maintain the sacred
groves throughout Tirvandor and regulate who may learn primal magic.

The Green Faith predates most organized religions, its traditions
extending back before written history. Members serve as spiritual guides
in rural areas, particularly in Aethoria where druids hold more cultural
authority than temple priests.

The organization maintains a delicate balance between civilization and
wilderness, acknowledging that human settlements can coexist with nature
while insisting on limits to expansion. They have significant political
influence in Aethoria and can mobilize formidable forces if natural
sites are threatened.

**Structure:**

The Green Faith is governed by a Council of Elders---seven druids, each
representing a different aspect of nature. Regional circles report to
the council, but individual druids maintain significant autonomy.
Decisions are made by consensus rather than decree.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 16: Religious Structures and Faith}}
\page

**Interests:**

-   Protecting ancient forests and sacred sites

-   Maintaining natural balance

-   Preventing ecological disasters

-   Teaching proper relationship with nature

-   Opposing excessive civilization spread

**The Academies of Moira**

Institutions of magical learning that combine religious devotion with
arcane study, the Academies train mages while instilling reverence for
knowledge and fate. Major academies exist in Silverpine and Aethermere.

The Academies sometimes clash with traditional religious authorities
over the role of magic in society. They view arcane and divine magic as
complementary rather than opposed, which puts them at odds with more
conservative temple hierarchies.

**The Lightbringers (Order of Aethor)**

The primary militant order of Aethor, the Lightbringers are
hierarchical, military-style paladins and clerics dedicated to
destroying undead and fiends, protecting the innocent, and spreading the
Liberator's light.

Their headquarters is in Aethermere, and they maintain chapters
throughout both continents. They are famous for their effectiveness
against supernatural evil and their sometimes insufferable
righteousness.

**Structure:**

-   Hierarchical, military-style organization

-   Ranks from initiate to Lord Commander

-   Report to the High Priestess of Aethor

-   Divided into regional chapters

**The Green Circle (Druids of Sylvara)**

The most powerful druidic organization, maintaining balance between
civilization and nature. They have significant political influence in
Aethoria and can mobilize formidable forces if threatened.

The Green Circle maintains the Wildgrove as their holiest site and
serves as the primary authority on matters of primal magic throughout
both continents.

**The Grave Wardens (Order of Mordain)**

Death clerics and undead hunters dedicated to Mordain, they ensure
proper burial rites, comfort the bereaved, and most importantly, destroy
undead wherever found. Grim but necessary, they command universal
respect---and fear.

### 16.2 The Divine Silence and Its Legacy


The period when the gods stopped answering prayers (approximately
2,400-2,200 BW) fundamentally changed divine-mortal relationships. Its
effects persist to the present day.

\column

**What Happened**

For roughly two hundred years, divine magic simply stopped working.
Clerics lost their powers. Paladins found their oaths unanswered.
Prayers went unheard. The gods, by all evidence, had departed or were
otherwise unable to respond.

The cause remains unknown. Various theories suggest:

-   The gods were fighting their own war on another plane

-   Mortals had committed some collective offense

-   Something was blocking the divine connection

-   The gods were testing mortal faith

-   A cosmic event temporarily severed divine access

When the gods returned, they provided no clear explanation. Different
faiths developed different interpretations, leading to theological
disputes that continue in the present.

**Lasting Effects**

*Trust Issues*

Some mortals never fully trusted the gods again. If they could abandon
their followers once, what prevents them from doing so again? This
skepticism manifests in various ways: philosophical movements that honor
the gods without fully depending on them, individuals who worship
pragmatically rather than devotionally, and persistent questions about
divine reliability.

*Rise of Arcane Magic*

When divine magic failed, arcane magic filled the void. Wizard schools
expanded, sorcerous bloodlines were cultivated, and magical research
accelerated. The relationship between divine and arcane traditions was
never quite the same---arcane practitioners retained the prestige gained
during the Silence, and some viewed their magic as more reliable than
that of clerics.

*New Covenants*

When the gods returned, they established new terms for granting power.
Clerics must be more devout, paladins more committed to their oaths. The
bar for divine favor rose significantly. Some interpret this as the gods
demanding greater commitment; others see it as the gods limiting their
exposure to unreliable followers.

*The Unanswered Questions*

Where did the gods go? Why did they return? Are they as powerful as they
claim? These questions haunt theological scholars. The gods' silence on
the matter itself speaks volumes---or perhaps says nothing at all.

*Diverse Interpretations*

Different faiths explain the Silence differently:

-   Thandros' followers suggest it was a test of civilizational
    endurance

-   Aethor's followers claim the gods withdrew so mortals could develop
    self-reliance

-   Moira's followers hint that it was fated and served purposes yet to
    be revealed

-   Some believe it proves the gods are fallible

-   Others maintain faith despite lacking explanations

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 16: Religious Structures and Faith}}
\page

### 16.3 Divine Magic in Practice


Divine magic in Tirvandor flows through ley lines like all magic, but is
shaped and directed by the relationship between mortal and deity.

**Clerics**

Clerics are granted power directly from their deity. They must pray
daily, follow their god's tenets, and actively advance their god's
interests. If they violate their divine code significantly, they lose
access to their powers until they atone.

The relationship is reciprocal but unequal. The god grants power; the
cleric serves as the god's agent in the mortal world. Most clerics
genuinely believe in their deity and serve willingly, but the power
dynamic remains.

**Paladins**

Paladins swear oaths that align with divine principles but represent
personal commitments rather than direct divine service. Their power
comes from the strength of their conviction as much as from any deity.

A paladin might serve Thandros without being a cleric of
Thandros---their oath of justice aligns with his principles without
requiring direct service. This makes paladins somewhat independent of
temple hierarchies, which creates occasional tension.

**Divine Soul Sorcerers**

Some individuals are born with an innate connection to divine energy,
often seen as chosen or blessed. They don't pray for power---it's
inherent to their nature. The gods may have selected them, or they may
simply have been born at the right confluence of cosmic forces.

Divine soul sorcerers occupy an unusual position in religious society.
They have divine power without being clergy, which some temples find
threatening and others find inspiring.

**Celestial Warlocks**

Those who make pacts with celestial beings (angels, archons, etc.)
access divine power through transactional relationships rather than
devotional ones. They agree to perform certain services in exchange for
certain powers.

This approach is viewed with suspicion by traditional clergy, who see it
as commodifying the sacred. Celestial warlocks counter that their
honesty about the exchange is more ethical than pretending divine
service is purely voluntary.

### 16.4 Faith and Culture by Region


**Thaldros**

Religion in Thaldros is organized, hierarchical, and public. The state
maintains close relationships with temple hierarchies, and religious
observance is considered a civic duty as much as a spiritual practice.

Written scriptures carry authority. Formal ceremonies mark religious
occasions. Temple hierarchies report to both religious and secular
authorities. Faith is expressed communally through public rituals and
collective worship.

Thandros naturally dominates in a culture that values law and order, but
all Seven are honored. The state church system regulates worship,
ensuring that religious authority supports rather than challenges
secular power.

**Aethoria**

Religion in Aethoria is mystical, personal, and diverse. Individual
temples operate independently, and spiritual practice is considered a
private matter between the individual and the divine.

Oral traditions carry as much weight as written texts. Druids serve as
spiritual guides in many communities, particularly rural ones. Personal
experience of the divine is valued over formal doctrine. Faith is
expressed through individual practice and small community rituals.

Aethor and Sylvara dominate in a culture that values freedom and nature,
but the emphasis on religious freedom means all faiths flourish.

**The Islands**

Island communities practice syncretic religion, blending eastern and
western traditions into practical faith focused on immediate needs. A
sailor might invoke Kalythra for storms, Kael for navigation, Sera for
healing, and local spirits for luck---all in the same voyage.

Faith in the islands is pragmatic. What works is what matters.
Theological disputes that consume mainland scholars are largely
irrelevant to those whose survival depends on placating whatever powers
govern wind and wave.

### 16.5 Interaction with Other Planes


The gods reside in the Celestial Realms---planes of existence adjacent
to the material world. However, they are not the only powers mortals
might encounter or serve.

**Archfey**

Powerful entities of the Feywild, archfey are neither gods nor mortals.
They offer pacts to warlocks, grant boons to those who please them, and
meddle in mortal affairs for reasons that may be incomprehensible. Some
communities worship particular archfey, though the Seven's temples
generally discourage this.

**Demon Princes**

Evil beings of the Abyss offer power to those desperate or corrupt
enough to accept. Their cults are suppressed throughout civilized
Tirvandor, but they persist in shadows, offering forbidden power at
terrible prices.

**Devil Archdukes**

Lawful evil entities of the Nine Hells offer more structured bargains
than demons---contracts rather than chaos. Their cults operate more
subtly, sometimes disguising themselves as legitimate organizations. The
line between a devil cult and a corrupt merchant guild can be
surprisingly thin.

{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 16: Religious Structures and Faith}}
\page

**Primordial Aspects**

Elemental entities from the elemental planes sometimes take interest in
mortal affairs. Those who serve them gain access to elemental magic, but
the relationship is impersonal---elements don't care about their
servants the way gods do.

**Great Old Ones**

Alien consciousnesses from beyond mortal understanding occasionally
touch Tirvandor. Their servants gain power through incomprehensible
connections, and their motives cannot be understood in mortal terms.
Most authorities consider Great Old One worship extremely dangerous,
though the entities themselves may not even notice their worshippers.

\column

*The gods of Tirvandor are real but not omnipotent. They have agendas,
make mistakes, and compete with each other---sometimes subtly, sometimes
openly. Mortals must navigate these divine politics while maintaining
their own agency and pursuing their own goals. The religious landscape
is complex, and simple answers are rare.*
