## Chapter 45: Common Folk and Supporting Characters


### 45.1 Marta Goodbarrel


**Title:** Owner of The Goodbarrel Inn

**Location:** Goldreach

**Age:** 67 (halfling)

A rotund, cheerful halfling woman who has run the Goodbarrel Inn for
thirty years. Her establishment serves as neutral ground where deals get
made---she hears everything and shares nothing. Former adventurer who
retired after losing her party to a dragon. Keeps a loaded crossbow
under the bar and knows how to use it.

Marta's inn attracts merchants, adventurers, and shadier characters
alike. She treats everyone the same: good food, fair prices, and
absolute discretion. The only rule is "no fighting inside"---violators
are banned for life, and in Goldreach, that's a serious social penalty.

**Secret:** Marta still has contacts from her adventuring days,
including a former party member who became a dragon. They correspond
occasionally.

### 45.2 Old Barrett


**Title:** Retired Adventurer, Village Elder

**Location:** Various (travels between villages)

**Age:** 73 (human)

A weathered old man who was a legendary adventurer forty years ago. Now
he runs a small shop and advises young adventurers, sharing hard-won
wisdom about dungeons, monsters, and treasure. Barrett knows more about
the dangerous places of Tirvandor than anyone should.

He was part of a famous adventuring party that included several people
who went on to positions of power. These old contacts occasionally ask
him for quiet favors, and he occasionally asks them for help on behalf
of promising young heroes he's mentoring.

**Secret:** Barrett's old party found something in a dungeon that they
agreed to never speak of. One of them broke that oath. The others died
within the year. Barrett is the last survivor, and he's never told
anyone what they found.

### 45.3 Watch Captain Gregor Ironhand

![45.3 Watch Captain Gregor Ironhand](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/tirvandor-npc-watch-captain-gregor-ironhand.jpg){width:200px,float:right,margin:5px}


**Title:** Captain of the Crossvale City Watch

**Location:** Crossvale

**Age:** 42 (human)

Born to a blacksmith and a seamstress, Gregor rose through the Watch
ranks through competence and stubborn honesty. He cannot be bribed---not
because he's rich, but because he genuinely believes in the law. Made
Watch Captain at 38 after his predecessor was murdered by the Syndicate.
He swore to clean up Crossvale and has been trying ever since.

Gregor commands 80 City Watch officers and reports to Burgher-Master
Wilhelm Von Handel. He has an informant---a street urchin named
Pip---who reports suspicious activity.

**Secret:** Gregor's older brother Marcus is "The Iron Hand"---a
Syndicate enforcer who handles their most violent problems. The brothers
haven't spoken in years. Gregor doesn't know his brother's criminal
identity. If he ever discovered the truth, it would break him---and
he'd still make the arrest.

### 45.4 Harbor Master Tobias Saltwind


**Title:** Harbor Master of Goldreach

**Location:** Goldreach Harbor

**Age:** 54 (human)

A barrel-chested man with a booming voice who controls everything that
enters or leaves Goldreach by sea. Tobias is scrupulously honest in his
official duties, which makes him unusual among port officials. He runs a
tight operation and commands the respect of both sailors and merchants.

Former naval officer who served with distinction before taking the
harbor position. His knowledge of ships, tides, and weather is
encyclopedic. Sailors trust his judgment about when it's safe to sail.

**Secret:** Tobias lost his son to a sea monster years ago. He quietly
funds expeditions to hunt such creatures and keeps a trophy room of
their remains in his basement.

### 45.5 Caravan Master Hassan


**Title:** Master of the Desert Routes

**Location:** Sundara and the Sundaran Expanse

**Age:** 45 (human)

The most successful caravan master in the Sundaran desert, Hassan knows
every oasis, every shortcut, and every danger between Sundara and the
coast. He charges premium prices but has never lost a caravan to bandits
or the elements.

Hassan employs a network of scouts, guards, and desert guides. He treats
his people well and they're fiercely loyal. Merchants pay extra to
travel with his caravans because the alternative---cheaper
operators---often end in disaster.

**Secret:** Hassan has an arrangement with several bandit tribes. He
pays them tribute, and they attack his competitors instead. It's pure
business, and he feels no guilt about it.

### 45.6 Burgher-Master Wilhelm Von Handel


**Title:** Burgher-Master of Crossvale

**Location:** Crossvale

**Age:** 58 (human)

The elected leader of Crossvale, Wilhelm is a former merchant who
entered politics to protect his business interests and discovered he had
a talent for governance. He's pragmatic rather than idealistic, willing
to make deals with anyone who can help Crossvale prosper.

Wilhelm maintains a delicate balance between the noble houses, merchant
guilds, and criminal elements that all want influence in Crossvale.
He's neither corrupt nor honest---he's practical, doing whatever keeps
the city running and the coin flowing.

**Secret:** Wilhelm knows the Syndicate operates in his city. He's made
a tacit arrangement: they don't cause public problems, he doesn't look
too hard for them. It keeps the peace, but it weighs on him.

### 45.7 Marcus Vrell


**Title:** Information Broker

**Location:** Varies (maintains offices in major cities)

**Age:** 39 (human)

A nondescript man with forgettable features---perfect for his
profession. Marcus can find information on almost any topic within a few
days. He knows someone in every major organization and maintains strict
neutrality, selling information to anyone who can pay.

Marcus charges based on the difficulty and danger of obtaining
information. Simple facts are cheap; secrets that could get people
killed are expensive. He never reveals his sources, and his information
is always accurate---his reputation depends on it.

**Secret:** Marcus maintains detailed files on his clients as insurance.
If anything happens to him, the files go to the most damaging possible
recipients.

### 45.8 Silas the Fence


**Title:** Receiver of Stolen Goods

**Location:** Goldreach (underground markets)

**Age:** 52 (halfling)

The most successful fence in western Tirvandor, Silas can move almost
any stolen goods and get fair prices for sellers. He operates from a
shifting network of locations, staying one step ahead of the law through
a combination of bribes, caution, and the fact that too many powerful
people rely on his services.

Silas has strict rules: no stolen children, no sacred relics from active
temples, and no goods that would bring down heat on his operation.
Everything else is fair game.

**Secret:** Silas is actually a retired Syndicate assassin who made
enough money to buy his way out. He keeps his old skills sharp, just in
case.

### 45.9 Elder Tremont


**Title:** Village Elder and Retired Priest

**Location:** Small village near Silverpine

**Age:** 81 (human)

A gentle old man who served as a priest of Sera for fifty years before
retiring to a small village. He now tends a modest shrine, advises young
people, and tries to do small kindnesses every day. The villagers
consider him a living saint, though he'd be embarrassed by the title.

Tremont has no combat abilities and no political power. What he has is
wisdom, kindness, and a lifetime of experience helping people through
their troubles. Adventurers sometimes seek him out for guidance, and he
always has time to listen.

**Secret:** In his youth, Tremont committed a terrible sin that drove
him to the priesthood in penance. He's never told anyone what it was,
and he's spent sixty years trying to balance the scales.

### 45.10 Pip


**Title:** Street Urchin and Informant

**Location:** Crossvale

**Age:** 12 (human)

A scrappy orphan who survives on the streets of Crossvale through quick
wits and quicker feet. Pip works as an informant for Watch Captain
Gregor, reporting suspicious activity in exchange for a few coins and
occasional protection. The kid sees everything and remembers it all.

Pip dreams of becoming a real adventurer someday. For now, surviving is
adventure enough. The street urchins of Crossvale have their own
society, and Pip is working their way up in it.

**Secret:** Pip witnessed a murder committed by a noble's son. They've
kept quiet out of fear, but the guilt is eating at them.

### 45.11 Master Glasswright Zara


**Title:** Master of the Sundaran Glasswright Guild

**Location:** Sundara

**Age:** 34 (human)

The youngest person ever to achieve the rank of Master Glasswright, Zara
creates works of art that sell for thousands of gold pieces. Her stained
glass windows grace temples and palaces across Tirvandor. High Priest
Al-Sahir blessed her workshop, and she credits him for her success.

Zara employs dozens of apprentices and journeymen. She's demanding but
fair, pushing her workers to excellence while ensuring they're
well-compensated. Her guild is the most prestigious craft organization
in Sundara.

**Secret:** Zara's gift for glasswork emerged after a fever nearly
killed her as a child. She sometimes sees visions in molten
glass---prophecies she's learned to encode in her artwork for those who
know how to read them.

### 45.12 The Iron Hand (Marcus Ironhand)

![45.12 The Iron Hand (Marcus Ironhand)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixologee/tirvandor/main/tirvandor-project/all_artwork/npcs/tirvandor-npc-brother-marcus.jpg){width:200px,float:right,margin:5px}


**Title:** Syndicate Enforcer

**Location:** Crossvale

**Age:** 45 (human)

A brutal enforcer who handles the Syndicate's most violent problems.
The Iron Hand earned his name through his signature method---crushing
hands in a vice. He's feared throughout the underworld as someone who
gets results without questions.

What no one knows is that the Iron Hand is Marcus Ironhand---brother to
Watch Captain Gregor. They haven't spoken in years, and Marcus has
carefully hidden his identity. He tells himself it's to protect Gregor,
but really, some small part of him is still ashamed.

**Secret:** Marcus still loves his brother. He's secretly intervened to
protect Gregor from Syndicate retaliation twice, at great personal risk.

# Part VIII: Creatures



{{pageNumber,auto}}
{{footnote Chapter 46: Border Creatures}}

\page

## Chapter 46: Border Creatures


The Contested Lands, the war-torn frontier between Thaldros and
Aethoria, has spawned unique creatures shaped by centuries of conflict.
The constant violence, lingering death, and instability have transformed
both the living and the dead into something distinct from what exists in
either nation's heartland.

These border creatures represent the cost of war made manifest, in
flesh, in spirit, and in the very land itself.

### 46.1 Border Bandit


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

Border bandits look like what they are: people at the end of their rope.
Thin from irregular meals, scarred from fights, wearing mismatched armor
and patched clothing taken from whoever had it last. Their eyes are
watchful, the gaze of prey animals that have learned to survive by
becoming predators themselves.

They carry whatever weapons they could acquire: battered swords, rusted
crossbows, improvised clubs. Nothing matches. Nothing is ceremonial.
Everything is functional, because dead bandits don't need pretty
equipment.

**Origins:**

Border bandits come from everywhere the war has touched. Some are
refugees who found no welcome in safer lands and turned to theft to
survive. Others are deserters from both armies, soldiers who decided
that death in battle was less appealing than the risks of banditry. Some
are opportunists who came to the Contested Lands specifically because
law doesn't reach here.

Most didn't choose this life. The war chose it for them.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

Bandits operate in small groups (usually five to fifteen) for mutual
protection. They stake out territories along trade routes and ambush
travelers who seem vulnerable enough to rob without excessive risk.

Despite their reputation, most border bandits prefer surrender to
slaughter. Dead victims can't be robbed again, and killing merchants
discourages future trade through their territory. Smart bandits take
enough to survive but leave enough that their victims don't seek
vengeance.

They know the terrain intimately, every cave, every ruin, every hidden
approach. This knowledge is their primary advantage against
better-equipped opponents. A bandit who survives long enough to learn
the land becomes genuinely dangerous.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Border bandits are survivors, and survivors are intelligent by
definition, the stupid ones died first. They maintain loose hierarchies
based on experience and success, following whoever keeps them alive and
fed.

Some groups maintain codes of conduct: don't harm children, don't kill
unless necessary, share equally. Others have abandoned such niceties.
The difference often determines whether a bandit group becomes a
tolerated nuisance or a hunted enemy.

Information passes quickly through bandit networks. They know which
merchants carry valuable cargo, which patrols take which routes, which
other groups are reliable allies or treacherous rivals.

**Abilities:**

Border bandits excel at concealment and ambush in their home terrain.
They know hiding spots invisible to outsiders, can move silently through
rubble and ruins, and strike with the desperate ferocity of people with
nothing left to lose.

When wounded, they often fight harder rather than fleeing, desperation
making them dangerous rather than cautious. But they're also practical;
most will surrender or flee if offered reasonable terms, preferring
survival to pointless death.

**Cultural Significance:**

In Thaldros and Aethoria alike, "border bandit" is a convenient label
for everyone who lives in the Contested Lands outside official
authority. This is unfair, many border dwellers are farmers, merchants,
or tradespeople trying to survive. But the stereotype persists.

Ironically, some bandits have become folk heroes among the dispossessed.
Stories circulate of bandit leaders who only target military convoys,
who share stolen wealth with starving villages, who represent resistance
against powers that have abandoned the border's people.

**Story Potential:**

-   The bandits who ambush the party turn out to be former soldiers
    fighting a guerrilla war against occupation

-   A bandit leader holds information vital to the party's mission, but
    won't share it without payment or service

-   The party must negotiate safe passage through bandit territory,
    playing different groups against each other

-   A seemingly simple bandit attack reveals that someone powerful is
    directing these "random" raids

### 46.2 Smuggler Captain


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

Smuggler captains dress to impress and disarm. They favor practical but
expensive clothing, quality leather, sturdy boots, travel cloaks that
conceal weapons while suggesting wealth. Their appearance says
"successful merchant" rather than "criminal," which is exactly the
point.

They move with easy confidence, hands always visible, smiles ready. The
best captains can convince border guards they're old friends, talk
their way past checkpoints, and negotiate with anyone from desperate
refugees to corrupt generals.

**Origins:**

The border between Thaldros and Aethoria is a maze of regulations,
tariffs, and prohibitions. Anything that's legal on one side is
restricted on the other. This creates profitable opportunities for those
willing to ignore borders entirely.

Smuggler captains emerged from this chaos, entrepreneurs who saw
opportunity in connecting supply with demand regardless of national
boundaries. Some began as legitimate merchants pushed into illegality by
impossible regulations. Others were always criminals who found a new
venue.

Most work for themselves or small networks rather than larger criminal
organizations, though the Shadow Syndicate and Thornwood Syndicate both
use smugglers for specific operations.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

Captains run operations that move people, goods, and information across
the border. They maintain networks of contacts on both sides: bribed
officials, sympathetic innkeepers, reliable guides, corrupt merchants
who ask no questions.

They're genuinely neutral in the continental conflict, they'll work
for anyone who pays. This neutrality is both professional principle and
practical necessity. Taking sides would cut off half their market.

Every captain maintains emergency plans: escape routes, hidden
resources, false identities for when things go wrong. Paranoia isn't a
flaw in this profession, it's a job requirement.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Successful smugglers are remarkably intelligent, combining merchant's
acumen with criminal's caution. They speak multiple languages,
understand economics, read people accurately, and plan for
contingencies.

They maintain loose professional networks, sharing information about
dangerous routes, reliable contacts, and treacherous customers.
Competition is fierce but rarely deadly, killing a rival smuggler is bad
for business and tends to attract unwanted attention.

Most captains genuinely honor their deals. Reputation is everything in
an illegal business; a smuggler known for betraying clients doesn't
stay in business long.

**Abilities:**

Captains are skilled negotiators who can read situations and people with
uncanny accuracy. They know when to charm, when to threaten, when to
bribe, and when to run. Many have genuinely supernatural ability to
propose bargains that opponents find difficult to refuse.

In combat, they're fast and slippery rather than powerful. They fight
to create escape opportunities, not to win battles. Every captain knows
that any fight they're in has already gone wrong.

Their true ability is their network. Given time, a smuggler captain can
arrange almost anything: safe passage, false documents, weapons,
information, even assassinations. They know people who know people.

**Cultural Significance:**

Both governments officially condemn smuggling while quietly relying on
it. Military commanders buy black-market supplies through smuggler
networks. Intelligence services pay for information that only smugglers
can provide. The condemnation is real; so is the dependency.

Among border dwellers, smugglers are often the only connection to goods
and services unavailable through legal channels. They bring medicine,
food, tools, and news. This makes them important community figures
regardless of their technical criminality.

**Story Potential:**

-   The party needs to cross the border discreetly; only a smuggler can
    get them through

-   A smuggler captain has information about enemy movements, but wants
    something in return

-   The party discovers their smuggler contact is playing both sides of
    the conflict

-   A smuggler's betrayal isn't what it seems, they're being
    blackmailed or threatened

### 46.3 War-Scarred Veteran


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

These veterans wear their history on their bodies. Scars cover what skin
shows, sword cuts, burn marks, wounds from weapons that shouldn't have
been survivable. Many are missing fingers, eyes, limbs, or pieces of
ears. Their joints ache. Their sleep is haunted.

But they move with deadly economy, never wasting motion, always
balanced. However broken their bodies, their combat instincts remain
razor-sharp.

They often wear well-maintained but outdated armor, equipment they've
repaired and modified over years of use. Their weapons are similarly
veteran: blade edges that have been sharpened until the metal is
noticeably thinner, hilts worn smooth by countless grips.

**Origins:**

The Contested Lands have seen fighting for over a century. Some veterans
have served in formal armies on one side or the other, discharged after
injuries made them "unfit for duty." Others were mercenaries who
fought for whoever paid, building decades of experience through
contracts.

Many simply survived where they shouldn't have. They're not special,
they're just the ones who didn't die. This perspective colors
everything they do.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

Veterans gravitate toward roles that use their skills without requiring
the physical demands of active campaigning. Some become mercenary
instructors, training new fighters in the hard lessons they learned
through experience. Others become guards, guides, or muscle for hire.

Some retreat entirely, becoming hermits in the border's wilds. They're
done with violence, until violence finds them, and old instincts
resurface.

They're cautious fighters, conserving energy and exploiting weaknesses.
They know that enthusiasm gets soldiers killed; discipline keeps them
alive. They'll retreat from fights they can't win and wait for better
opportunities.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Years of survival have made veterans cunning and perceptive. They read
battlefields instinctively, seeing cover, escape routes, and tactical
advantages that others miss. They understand violence in ways that
civilians never will.

Veterans recognize each other instantly, something in the eyes, the
stance, the way they scan rooms when entering. Informal networks exist
among them, sharing information about contracts, threats, and
opportunities.

Many struggle with what they've seen and done. Drink, nightmares,
sudden rages, an inability to feel safe, these are common. Some find
peace; others never do.

**Abilities:**

Veterans are extraordinarily difficult to kill. They've survived wounds
that should have been fatal, learned to fight through pain and
exhaustion, and developed an instinct for self-preservation that borders
on supernatural.

Fear doesn't affect them, they've seen worse. Intimidation attempts
usually fail; they've faced death too many times to be frightened by
threats.

Their combat skills are refined by decades of practice. They may not be
the strongest or fastest fighters, but they're efficient, no wasted
movement, no flashy techniques, just practical lethality.

**Cultural Significance:**

In both nations, veterans are uncomfortable reminders of the war's
human cost. They're respected in theory but often avoided in practice.
Their presence makes civilians uncomfortable, living proof that war
breaks people even when they survive.

Among soldiers, veterans are either revered or resented. Some see them
as fonts of wisdom; others see them as reminders of their own potential
fate. A veteran's advice about survival is usually correct but rarely
welcome.

**Story Potential:**

-   A veteran holds crucial knowledge about an old battle or buried
    secret in the Contested Lands

-   The party needs a guide through dangerous territory, only a veteran
    knows the safe paths

-   A respected veteran is being hunted by both sides for something they
    witnessed

-   The party must convince a retired veteran to take up arms one final
    time

### 46.4 Border Wraith


**Type:** Undead (incorporeal spirit)

**Physical Description:**

Border wraiths are darkness given form, shadows that move against the
light, cold spots in the air that speak of violent death. They retain
vague humanoid shapes, echoes of the soldiers they were in life, though
their features are indistinct, constantly shifting.

When they manifest fully, witnesses report seeing ghostly armor,
spectral weapons, faces frozen in final expressions of agony or rage.
They carry the marks of their deaths: phantom wounds that weep shadow
instead of blood, translucent forms pierced by arrows that are no longer
there.

Their presence chills the air noticeably. Breath frosts. Water freezes.
Living creatures feel sudden dread, their bodies recognizing death
before their minds do.

**Origins:**

When soldiers die in the Contested Lands, especially when they die
violently, in great numbers, with unfinished business or overwhelming
emotion, some don't pass on. The centuries of bloodshed have saturated
certain areas with death energy, making it easier for spirits to
persist.

Border wraiths form from these trapped spirits. They're bound to the
region where they died, unable to pass on, unable to rest. Their
existence is a perpetual echo of their final moments: the battle that
killed them plays on repeat in their shattered consciousness.

Some retain fragments of their former identity, names, loyalties, final
words. These can sometimes be reached, reasoned with, even laid to rest.
Others have lost everything but rage and hunger.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

Wraiths are drawn to violence. Battle attracts them like blood attracts
sharks. They appear during skirmishes and ambushes, feeding on death,
sometimes participating in the carnage themselves.

They hunt at night, when their power is greatest. Sunlight weakens them
significantly; most remain hidden during day, emerging from walls or
floors at dusk.

When they first manifest, wraiths sometimes speak, a single phrase from
their death, a name, a fragment of orders. This echo of war gives
witnesses momentary insight into battles that might be centuries old.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Most wraiths retain only fragments of intelligence. They recognize the
living as enemies or prey, can use basic tactics, and remember enough of
combat to fight effectively. But they're not truly conscious, they're
patterns of violence playing on repeat.

Wraiths cluster around the most saturated areas, forming loose
collections that might look like spectral units. They don't coordinate
deliberately, but their shared patterns sometimes create the appearance
of tactics.

Rarely, a wraith retains more of its former self. These exceptional
cases might be reached through negotiation, convinced to pass on through
completing unfinished business, or (unfortunately) becoming more
dangerous due to retained intelligence.

**Abilities:**

Border wraiths can pass through solid objects, making walls and doors
meaningless obstacles. They strike with incorporeal claws that drain
life force itself, weakening victims in ways that physical healing
cannot address.

Worse, wraiths can create more of their kind. Those they kill violently
might rise as lesser spirits under the wraith's instinctive control. A
single wraith that finds victims can quickly become several.

They're bound to the border region where they died. Force a wraith
beyond these boundaries, and it suffers increasing agony, eventually
dissipating if kept away long enough.

**Cultural Significance:**

Both nations acknowledge border wraiths as real threats, though they
rarely discuss them openly. Military commanders factor wraith activity
into campaign planning; smart officers avoid night battles in regions
known for heavy historical casualties.

Among border dwellers, wraiths are simply part of life, another danger
to avoid, like bandits or bad weather. Communities learn which areas are
haunted and stay away. Travelers are warned about especially dangerous
regions.

The Order of Moira considers wraith-laying sacred work. Their priests
sometimes venture into the Contested Lands specifically to consecrate
haunted ground and help trapped spirits pass on.

**Story Potential:**

-   A wraith retains crucial information about a historical event, but
    communicating with it is dangerous

-   The party must cross a haunted battlefield at night, avoiding or
    fighting the spectral army that manifests

-   Someone is deliberately creating conditions that produce new
    wraiths, weaponizing the dead

-   A wraith recognizes one of the party members as connected to its
    living past

### 46.5 Contested Land Elemental


**Type:** Elemental

**Physical Description:**

These elementals embody the border's broken nature. Their bodies are
earth and stone, but the composition is chaotic, layers of soil from
both nations visible like geological strata, minerals that shouldn't
exist together fused into unstable amalgamation.

They're massive, roughly humanoid, averaging twelve feet tall. Their
features shift constantly as their substance reorganizes itself. One arm
might be Thaldros granite; the other, Aethorian sandstone. Their eyes
are voids where the earth couldn't agree on what it should be.

When they move, the ground trembles. Their footsteps leave craters. They
smell of freshly turned earth and ancient stone, and underneath, the
copper tang of blood.

**Origins:**

The Contested Lands have been soaked in blood for centuries. The
constant violence has poisoned the earth itself, saturating it with
death and rage until the land developed something like consciousness, or
at least, instinct.

Contested land elementals are the earth's immune response. They form
where the damage is worst, arising from soil mixed with the blood of too
many battles. They exist to protect their domain from further
destruction.

Unlike true elementals that embody a pure element, these creatures
embody conflict itself. Their substance is inherently unstable because
it's composed of materials that were never meant to mix.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

These elementals are territorial in a literal sense, they defend
territory. Specifically, they attack those who damage the land: armies
that dig trenches, travelers who start fires, anyone who spills blood on
ground that's already saturated with it.

They're neutral toward peaceful travelers who don't disturb their
domain. Someone walking through contested earth without violence might
never see an elemental at all. But start a battle, build fortifications,
or desecrate the land further, and the earth itself rises up in
response.

They're most active in areas that have seen the heaviest fighting. Old
battlefields, ruined fortresses, and mass graves are their preferred
territory.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Contested land elementals possess limited intelligence, about as much as
a guard animal. They recognize threats, distinguish between harmful and
harmless behavior, and can be avoided by those who understand their
triggers.

They don't communicate in any traditional sense, though some druids
claim to have established empathy with them. What they receive is mostly
emotion: rage, protectiveness, exhaustion, grief.

These elementals are solitary; the land rarely produces more than one in
a given area. When their territory overlaps with another's, they simply
ignore each other.

**Abilities:**

These elementals move through earth and stone as easily as fish through
water. They emerge from below without warning, striking before targets
know they're present.

Their forms are unstable, occasionally erupting in small explosions when
struck. They can cause localized earthquakes that knock targets prone
and transform the terrain into difficult footing.

They're particularly hostile toward those who damage structures or
earth, siege engineers, miners, and arsonists tend to draw their
attention quickly.

**Cultural Significance:**

Military commanders on both sides have learned to factor contested land
elementals into their planning. Major battles in certain regions
guarantee elemental response, which sometimes damages both armies
equally.

Some scholars theorize that the elementals represent the land's attempt
to end the war by making it too costly to continue. If so, the land is
losing, the war continues despite elemental interference.

Druids view these elementals with complicated reverence. They're
natural spirits of a kind, but they're also aberrations, products of
unnatural violence against the earth. Some druids work to heal the
conditions that create them; others believe they should be left alone as
guardians.

**Story Potential:**

-   The party must cross elemental territory without triggering a
    response

-   An elemental has awakened near a strategic location, threatening
    both armies equally

-   Someone has found a way to control or direct contested land
    elementals, and is using them as weapons

-   The party discovers that the elementals are guarding something
    buried deep underground

### 46.6 Refugee Mob


**Type:** Humanoid swarm (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

A refugee mob isn't a creature in the traditional sense, it's
desperation given collective form. Dozens or hundreds of people, pushed
past breaking point, acting as one terrified, angry organism.

Individually, they're just people: families, workers, farmers displaced
by war. Their clothes are worn, their faces gaunt, their eyes showing
the empty exhaustion of those who've lost everything. Children cling to
parents. Elderly struggle to keep up. The sick and injured are carried
by those who can still walk.

But when fear or rage ignites them, they become something else. A mass
of reaching hands, screaming voices, crushing bodies. The individuals
disappear into the crowd.

**Origins:**

The Contested Lands produce refugees constantly. Villages caught between
armies are destroyed. Cities change hands and populations flee. People
who had homes, jobs, and lives become homeless wanderers with nothing
but what they can carry.

Most refugee groups remain peaceful, too exhausted and traumatized for
violence. But sometimes a spark ignites them: a perceived injustice, a
denial of desperately needed resources, a demagogue who channels their
anger. The result is a mob.

Mobs don't form from evil; they form from desperation. These are
ordinary people driven to extraordinary behavior by circumstances beyond
their control.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

Mobs are inherently unstable. They form quickly around triggering
events, act violently, and dissipate when the energy is spent or hope is
offered. The same group might be a peaceful refugee column one hour and
a violent mob the next.

They overwhelm through numbers rather than skill. Individual mob members
aren't dangerous; the collective is. They target obvious threats and
symbols of whatever authority has wronged them.

Critically, mobs can be calmed. Offering food, safety, or hope can
defuse them. Addressing legitimate grievances, really addressing them,
not just promising to, transforms mobs back into refugees. The violence
isn't natural; it's a response to unnatural conditions.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Mobs have a kind of collective intelligence, or collective stupidity,
depending on perspective. They respond to emotional cues, follow whoever
seems most confident, and abandon leaders who show weakness.

Individual mob members often have no idea what the group is doing until
afterward. The crowd psychology takes over; people do things they'd
never do alone. This isn't an excuse, but it is an explanation.

After a mob disperses, participants often experience shame and horror at
their actions. They were themselves; they also weren't. The experience
is traumatic for everyone involved, victims and participants alike.

**Abilities:**

A mob's power is simple: numbers. They can overwhelm defenses, swarm
individual targets, and deal significant damage through sheer collective
force.

They're also dangerously unpredictable. Panic can turn a mob against
itself; they might stampede away from threats, trampling their own
members. Fear makes them dangerous to themselves as well as others.

**Cultural Significance:**

Both nations fear mob violence while doing little to address its root
causes. Refugees are treated as problems to be contained rather than
people to be helped. This creates the desperation that enables mobs to
form, a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Soldiers on both sides have disturbing stories about mob encounters.
Killing refugees, even rioters, haunts those who do it. The violence is
rarely clean or justified-feeling.

Priests and healers sometimes specialize in mob defusing, walking into
crowds alone and trusting that genuine compassion can reach desperate
people. This is heroically dangerous but sometimes works.

**Story Potential:**

-   The party must calm a mob before soldiers arrive and massacre them

-   Someone is deliberately provoking mobs to destabilize the region

-   A mob is approaching a location the party must defend, how do they
    respond?

-   The party discovers that a "mob attack" was actually something
    else entirely

### 46.7 Scavenger Ghoul


**Type:** Undead

**Physical Description:**

Scavenger ghouls are gaunt, twisted things that were once humanoid but
have been warped by undeath and constant corpse-feeding. Their skin is
gray and tight over prominent bones. Their fingers have elongated into
claws. Their teeth have multiplied and sharpened into multiple rows of
tearing fangs.

They smell of death, old death, new death, every death in between. Their
eyes have a faint phosphorescent glow that's visible in darkness. They
move in a hunched, scuttling manner, closer to animals than the people
they once were.

Most retain some vestiges of the clothing they died in, though it's
usually rotted to rags. Some still wear armor that's rusted to their
flesh.

**Origins:**

The Contested Lands are a ghoul paradise. Constant violence produces
constant corpses. Where there are corpses, ghouls thrive.

These particular ghouls have adapted to battlefield scavenging. They're
drawn to the aftermath of violence, not the violence itself, but its
products. They've evolved (if undead can be said to evolve) to
specialize in finding and consuming the dead.

Most scavenger ghouls were created from people who died in the region
and rose due to exposure to concentrated death energy. Others wandered
in from elsewhere, drawn by the abundance of food.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

Scavenger ghouls hunt in packs, typically four to twelve individuals.
They follow armies at a distance, lurking near battlefields, waiting for
the fighting to end and the feasting to begin.

They're patient. They'll wait days for an opportunity, hiding in ruins
or underground until the living leave. They don't attack armed groups
if they can avoid it; corpses don't fight back, and ghouls prefer easy
meals.

But they're also opportunistic. Wounded travelers, isolated soldiers,
anyone weak enough to be easy prey, all are potential food sources. They
prefer dead flesh, but they're willing to kill to eat when hungry
enough.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Scavenger ghouls retain limited intelligence, enough to use pack
tactics, recognize danger, and communicate through hissing and
chittering sounds. They're cunning predators but not sophisticated
thinkers.

Pack hierarchies exist based on age and strength. Older ghouls lead;
younger ones follow. Disputes are settled through displays of aggression
that rarely result in actual combat, ghouls don't waste food fighting
each other.

They have no culture, no goals beyond feeding, no existence beyond
hunger. If the wars ever truly ended and corpses became scarce,
scavenger ghouls would spread into other regions seeking food, or die
out entirely.

**Abilities:**

Scavenger ghouls share standard ghoul capabilities: paralyzing touch
that immobilizes prey, darkvision that allows night hunting, and
resistance to many attacks that harm living creatures.

They've developed enhanced ability to locate corpses and wounded
creatures. They can smell death from remarkable distances and track prey
through scent alone.

Their pack tactics make them more dangerous than their individual
weakness suggests. They coordinate attacks, with some ghouls
immobilizing prey while others feed. They're also capable of healing by
consuming corpses, even mid-combat.

**Cultural Significance:**

Both armies consider ghoul infestations a logistical problem requiring
regular extermination. Leaving battlefields unattended guarantees ghoul
population growth; neither side wants expanding ghoul packs near their
supply lines.

Burial becomes critical in ghoul territory. Bodies must be burned,
buried deep, or consecrated, anything to deny ghouls easy food and
prevent new ghouls from rising. This adds cost and complexity to an
already expensive war.

Among civilians, ghouls are simply another horror the war has spawned.
Parents use them to frighten children into obedience: "Stay inside
after dark, or the ghouls will get you."

**Story Potential:**

-   A ghoul pack has grown large enough to threaten a settlement

-   The party must recover something from a battlefield before ghouls
    arrive

-   Someone is deliberately feeding ghouls to build an undead army

-   A ghoul pack's behavior suggests they're being directed by
    something intelligent

### 46.8 Territorial Drake


**Type:** Dragon (lesser)

**Physical Description:**

Territorial drakes are smaller cousins to true dragons, about the size
of a large horse, with wingless serpentine bodies, powerful legs, and
long tails. Their scales range from dusty brown to mottled gray,
providing natural camouflage in the rocky ruins they prefer.

Their heads are wedge-shaped, with forward-facing eyes that provide
excellent depth perception for ambush hunting. Multiple rows of serrated
teeth fill jaws capable of crushing armor. Their claws are hooked for
climbing and grasping prey.

Despite lacking wings, they're excellent climbers, scaling vertical
surfaces with ease. They often attack from above, dropping onto prey
from ruins or cliff faces.

**Origins:**

Drakes have always existed in Tirvandor, but the Contested Lands have
shaped a particular variety. The endless ruins provide perfect habitat,
elevated perches, protected dens, abundant prey (both animal and
humanoid).

Territorial drakes claimed these spaces as war destroyed former human
settlements. They've thrived in the chaos, growing more numerous and
aggressive as they learned to prey on refugees, soldiers, and travelers.

Some scholars believe they were originally domesticated, war mounts or
guard animals from pre-war settlements. Others argue they're simply
wild drakes that adapted to available territory.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

True to their name, these drakes fiercely defend claimed territories. A
single drake might control several square miles of ruins, attacking
anything that enters without permission.

They hunt through ambush, preferring to strike from concealment rather
than chase prey openly. Their camouflage and climbing ability make them
surprisingly difficult to spot until they attack.

Drakes pair for life, with mated couples sharing territory. They produce
clutches of two to four eggs annually; juveniles are driven out after
reaching maturity to establish their own territories.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Territorial drakes are intelligent for animals, roughly equivalent to
wolves or great apes. They can learn to recognize specific individuals,
understand simple concepts, and be trained for specific tasks.

They understand Draconic instinctively, responding to commands in that
language even without specific training. Some mercenary bands have
exploited this to domesticate drakes as mounts or war beasts.

Wild drakes communicate through roars, body language, and scent marking.
Their territorial calls carry for miles, warning other drakes of claimed
boundaries.

**Abilities:**

Drakes are powerful ambush predators. Their initial strike from
concealment is devastating, powerful jaws combined with raking claws can
bring down prey much larger than themselves.

Their tail attacks can knock opponents prone, creating openings for
follow-up bites. They coordinate with pack members when present, with
some drakes distracting prey while others strike.

When threatened, they can emit a territorial roar that alerts other
drakes in the area and provides temporary coordination bonuses to nearby
allies.

**Cultural Significance:**

Drake-hide armor is prized for its toughness and natural camouflage.
Hunters who can bring down territorial drakes command premium prices for
their hides, though the danger makes such hunts rare.

Some mercenary companies have successfully domesticated drakes as
mounts. These drake-riders are elite units, expensive to maintain but
devastatingly effective in rough terrain where conventional cavalry
can't operate.

Among border dwellers, drakes are simply dangerous wildlife to be
avoided. Communities learn which ruins are drake territory and stay
away.

**Story Potential:**

-   Drake eggs are valuable; the party is hired to retrieve some

-   A particularly large drake has claimed territory that blocks a
    critical route

-   Someone is training drakes for military use, who, and for what
    purpose?

-   The party discovers that drakes are more intelligent than commonly
    believed

### 46.9 War Beast


**Type:** Beast

**Physical Description:**

War beasts are massive predators, wolves, hunting cats, or war dogs,
bred and trained for military use. They average six feet at the
shoulder, with heavy muscle, powerful jaws, and coats that range from
dark gray to mottled brown depending on breeding lineage.

Their eyes show unusual intelligence for animals, the result of
selective breeding over generations. Scars from training and combat mark
most specimens. Their teeth and claws are larger than natural, another
result of deliberate breeding programs.

Domesticated war beasts wear barding and collars marking their military
unit. Feral specimens have often torn away such gear but may still bear
harness marks in their fur.

**Origins:**

Both Thaldros and Aethoria maintain war beast programs, breeding
predators for military application. These programs have run for
centuries, producing animals that are larger, smarter, and more
aggressive than their wild ancestors.

War beasts are trained from birth to follow commands, attack on order,
and protect their handlers. They form bonds with their assigned soldiers
that border on supernatural loyalty.

But war is chaos. Handlers die. Units scatter. Beasts escape or are
abandoned. The Contested Lands are home to substantial populations of
feral war beasts, dangerous predators with combat training and no human
masters.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

Domesticated war beasts are extensions of their handlers, disciplined,
obedient, focused on assigned tasks. They can follow complex commands,
distinguish friend from enemy, and execute military tactics.

Feral war beasts retain their training while losing their restraint.
They hunt in packs using military tactics, flanking, ambush, coordinated
strikes. They're more dangerous than wild predators because they think
like soldiers.

They've established territories throughout the Contested Lands,
competing with other predators and sometimes cooperating with each
other. Packs from the same original unit sometimes reunite, combining
into larger groups.

**Intelligence and Society:**

War beasts are remarkably intelligent, smarter than any natural
predator, approaching the problem-solving ability of primates. They can
learn new commands, adapt to unfamiliar situations, and even demonstrate
limited planning ability.

Feral packs maintain hierarchies similar to wolf packs, with dominant
pairs leading and subordinates following. Inter-pack conflicts occur but
rarely result in deaths, the animals seem to recognize that killing each
other wastes resources.

They can be re-domesticated if handled properly, though the process is
dangerous and time-consuming. Some mercenary companies specialize in
capturing and retraining feral war beasts.

**Abilities:**

War beasts are trained killers. They know how to knock targets prone,
coordinate with pack members, and focus on vulnerable enemies. Their
intimidating howls can paralyze opponents with fear, a deliberately bred
trait.

They're particularly dangerous against frightened targets, having been
trained to recognize and exploit fear responses. Those who panic when
facing war beasts often die quickly.

Their pack tactics make them far more dangerous than individual strength
would suggest. A single war beast is manageable; a pack of five is a
serious threat to armed groups.

**Cultural Significance:**

War beast handlers are specialized military roles in both nations. The
bond between handler and beast is celebrated in military tradition;
losing a war beast is considered equivalent to losing a comrade.

Feral war beasts are viewed with complicated feelings. They're
dangerous pests, yes, but they're also abandoned soldiers, victims of
the same war that creates human refugees. Some people can't bring
themselves to kill them.

The existence of feral populations is a minor scandal for both
militaries. Their breeding programs are supposed to produce loyal
servants, not uncontrolled threats. Neither nation admits how many
beasts have escaped over the centuries.

**Story Potential:**

-   A feral pack is threatening a settlement; can they be captured
    rather than killed?

-   The party must navigate territory controlled by war beast packs

-   Someone is capturing feral war beasts, who, and for what purpose?

-   A war beast recognizes a party member's military insignia and
    responds to commands

### 46.10 Haunted Battlefield


**Type:** Hazard (environmental undead manifestation)

**Physical Description:**

A haunted battlefield doesn't look particularly different from any
other war-torn land at first glance. Churned earth, scattered debris,
perhaps some remaining equipment and bones. The vegetation is often dead
or stunted, but that's common in the Contested Lands.

The difference becomes apparent at night, or sometimes at dawn or dusk,
when the light catches at odd angles. Ghostly figures flicker into view.
Phantom weapons clash. Screams echo from nowhere. The battle that
happened here is still happening, endlessly repeated in spiritual echo.

During full manifestation, the entire battlefield becomes visible:
spectral armies clashing, phantom siege engines launching ethereal
projectiles, the whole tragedy replaying for anyone unfortunate enough
to witness it.

**Origins:**

When enough people die violently in one place, when their fear and rage
and pain saturate the earth, when the moment of death is so overwhelming
that it leaves permanent impressions on reality, haunted battlefields
form.

They're not locations with many ghosts; they're locations that have
become ghosts. The land itself is haunted, the ground remembering trauma
it can't forget.

The Contested Lands have dozens of haunted battlefields, some dating
back centuries. New ones form periodically as particularly brutal
engagements add to the region's collection of horrors.

**Behavior and Ecology:**

Haunted battlefields are static, the horror doesn't spread, doesn't
migrate. But within their boundaries, they're extraordinarily
dangerous.

The battlefield "activates" at irregular intervals, though night is
most common. Living creatures within the area experience the battle as
if present, psychic damage from ghostly weapons, overwhelming terror
from phantom charges, the risk of being pulled into the reenactment
itself.

Spectral soldiers manifest during activation, attacking the living on
instinct. These aren't intelligent undead, they're impressions,
echoes, fragments of people who died here. But echoes can still kill.

**Intelligence and Society:**

The battlefield itself has no intelligence, it's a phenomenon, not a
creature. The spectral soldiers that manifest have even less: they're
barely conscious, following the same patterns they followed in their
final battle.

Sometimes, stronger spirits emerge from the general chaos, officers,
heroes, or particularly emotional deaths that left clearer impressions.
These might be briefly capable of communication or recognition before
dissolving back into the general horror.

The battlefields seem to have memory of a sort. Some respond more
violently to soldiers wearing specific insignia, suggesting they
"remember" who fought whom.

**Abilities:**

Anyone within a haunted battlefield when it activates experiences the
battle directly. Phantom weapons cause psychic damage that feels
completely real. Spectral charges can knock victims prone. The
overwhelming sensory assault leaves survivors shaken and disoriented.

The battlefield can spontaneously generate spectral soldiers, not true
ghosts, but temporary manifestations that attack and eventually
dissolve. It can also summon phantom armies: waves of spectral
combatants that overwhelm through numbers.

Consecration suppresses battlefield activity temporarily. Priests can
create safe zones within haunted areas through funeral rites, though the
suppression is limited in duration and radius.

**Cultural Significance:**

Both nations recognize haunted battlefields as navigation hazards and
military complications. Campaign planning must account for battlefield
locations; fighting within one risks catastrophic supernatural
casualties.

The Order of Moira considers battlefield consecration sacred work. Teams
of priests periodically venture into the Contested Lands specifically to
lay battlefields to rest. This requires performing comprehensive funeral
rites for all the dead, identified and unidentified, while defending
against the battlefield's manifestations.

Some battlefields have been consecrated repeatedly but always reawaken.
Scholars debate whether permanent pacification is possible or whether
some sites are simply too saturated with death to ever be cleansed.

**Story Potential:**

-   The party must cross a haunted battlefield, what route minimizes
    exposure?

-   A battlefield is growing, absorbing new deaths and expanding its
    boundaries

-   Someone wants to weaponize a haunted battlefield, draw enemies into
    it deliberately

-   The spirits trapped in a battlefield hold crucial information about
    an ancient conflict

-   A battlefield contains something that must be retrieved before it
    can be consecrated

*End of Chapter 41: Border Creatures*
