## Chapter 49: Iron Guild Mercenaries


The Iron Guild is Tirvandor's premier mercenary organization,
professional soldiers who serve only the contract. Unlike ideologically
motivated fighters on either side of the continental conflict, Guild
members are pragmatic professionals who've made violence their trade.

From fresh recruits learning the harsh realities of mercenary life to
legendary figures who've shaped the profession itself, Iron Guild
members represent a different kind of warrior: one defined by
competence, honor (of a particular sort), and absolute dedication to
completing contracted work.

### 49.1 Guild Recruit


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

Guild recruits look like people trying very hard to look professional.
Their equipment is standard issue, functional but not personalized.
Their armor often fits imperfectly, not yet adjusted to their bodies.
They move with trained precision that hasn't yet become natural,
following protocols consciously rather than instinctively.

They're typically young, though some older recruits exist, career
changers, veterans from other militaries, or people who came to
mercenary work through necessity. What they share is newness: that
particular combination of eagerness and uncertainty that marks the
inexperienced.

**Origins:**

The Iron Guild accepts recruits from many backgrounds. Some are
farmers' children seeking fortune. Others are minor nobles without
inheritance. Some are deserters from national armies who prefer
mercenary work to their former service. A few are criminals seeking
legitimacy, the Guild doesn't ask about pasts.

Recruitment involves basic screening: can the applicant fight, follow
orders, and work with others? Those who pass enter a probationary period
of training and supervised contracts. Those who fail wash out, or die.

The Guild charges no recruitment fees; instead, recruits work at reduced
pay until they've proven themselves. This ensures the Guild invests in
those it trains while weeding out those who can't perform.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Recruits follow protocols exactly as taught, because they don't yet
know when deviation is appropriate. They fight in formation, support
their partners, and retreat when ordered. Initiative is discouraged at
this level; following instructions correctly is rewarded.

They're notably steadier than untrained fighters of similar skill.
Guild training emphasizes psychological conditioning: don't panic,
don't run, trust your training. This conditioning gives recruits an
edge over equally skilled but less disciplined opponents.

Recruits are assigned to veteran mentors who supervise their early
contracts. These mentors are responsible for keeping recruits alive long
enough to become useful, and for identifying those who won't make it.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Recruits occupy the bottom of Guild hierarchy. They do the worst jobs,
receive the smallest shares, and are reminded constantly that they
haven't earned full membership yet. This creates strong motivation to
improve.

They form tight bonds with their cohort, other recruits who joined at
the same time. These relationships often persist throughout careers,
creating cross-company connections that benefit the Guild as a whole.

Most recruits feel a mix of pride (they're in the Guild) and insecurity
(they haven't proven themselves yet). Smart ones focus on learning;
foolish ones try to prove themselves too quickly and often die doing so.

**Abilities:**

Recruits are trained fighters, better than militia but not yet
exceptional. Their primary advantage is psychological conditioning that
makes them resistant to fear when fighting alongside allies.

Their professional training distinguishes them from untrained fighters
of similar combat skill. They know tactics, recognize signals, and
respond predictably to commands, all valuable in group combat.

**Cultural Significance:**

Guild recruits represent the mercenary profession's accessibility.
Anyone with basic capability can join and potentially rise through merit
rather than birth. This appeals to those without other prospects.

They're also reminders that mercenary work is genuinely dangerous.
Recruit mortality rates are significant. Those glossy recruitment
pitches about fortune and glory don't mention how many recruits die on
their first contracts.

**Story Potential:**

-   Recruits provide information about Guild operations they've
    observed

-   A recruit cohort is in over their head and needs help

-   Someone the party knows has joined the Guild as a recruit

-   Recruits assigned to oppose the party might be convinced to switch
    sides

### 49.2 Veteran Mercenary


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

Veterans look like survivors. Their equipment is personalized,
modifications and additions accumulated over years of contracts. Their
armor bears repair marks where damage was fixed. Their weapons show wear
patterns from actual use rather than training.

They move with economical confidence. No wasted motion. No unnecessary
display. They've learned what matters and discarded what doesn't.
Their eyes are watchful but not paranoid, the assessment has become
automatic.

Most bear visible scars. Some are missing fingers, ears, or eyes. These
marks are neither hidden nor displayed; they're simply facts of the
profession.

**Origins:**

Veterans are recruits who survived. That simple fact makes them
valuable, the Guild's training combined with actual field experience
produces competent, reliable soldiers.

Reaching veteran status typically requires three to five years of active
contract work. Those who achieve it have demonstrated both combat
capability and the judgment to know when fighting is and isn't
appropriate.

Many veterans have served on both sides of various conflicts at
different times. This isn't considered problematic, professional
soldiers go where contracts take them.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Veterans fight efficiently rather than dramatically. They know that
surviving battles matters more than winning them impressively. They take
cover, conserve energy, and avoid fair fights when unfair ones are
available.

They're comfortable with extended operations, long marches, poor
conditions, uncertain supply. Experience has taught them how to function
when circumstances are less than ideal.

In combat, they prefer to work with partners they know. Veteran pairs or
small teams coordinate almost telepathically, having practiced together
until cooperation became instinct.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Veterans occupy the Guild's middle tier. They've proven themselves but
haven't yet achieved leadership positions. Many are content to remain
at this level, not everyone wants command responsibility.

They maintain professional networks across Guild companies. Veterans
who've served together remain connected, sharing information about
contracts, employers, and conditions. This informal network is
surprisingly effective.

Most veterans have complicated relationships with civilian life.
They've been away too long, done too much, to fit comfortably in normal
society. The Guild becomes their community.

**Abilities:**

Veterans are experienced fighters with practical skills developed
through actual combat. They know how to survive, literally. Their
resistance to battlefield diseases and poisons reflects bodies that have
adapted to campaign conditions.

Their tactical retreat capability reflects hard-won wisdom: knowing when
to disengage is as important as knowing when to fight. Veterans who
didn't learn this lesson didn't become veterans.

**Cultural Significance:**

Veterans are the Guild's backbone. Captains and elites get glory;
veterans get the work done. Their reliability is what makes the Guild's
reputation valuable.

They represent what mercenary careers actually look like: not glamorous
legend, but steady competence applied over years. Most mercenaries who
survive long enough become veterans. Most never become more.

**Story Potential:**

-   Veterans provide experienced perspective on military situations

-   A veteran recognizes someone or something from a past contract

-   Veterans assigned to guard something might be negotiated with
    professionally

-   A veteran is trying to leave the profession and needs help

### 49.3 Guild Enforcer


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

Enforcers are imposing by design. They're selected partly for size and
presence, then trained to maximize intimidation. Heavy armor, large
weapons, and practiced scowls create impressions intended to make
confrontation unnecessary.

They're notably larger than typical Guild members, deliberate
recruitment preference. Their equipment is maintained to parade
standards, projecting Guild authority. They move with the controlled
threat of people capable of violence who prefer not to use it.

**Origins:**

Enforcers are veterans selected for internal security duties. They
police the Guild itself, ensuring contracts are honored, disputes are
settled according to Guild rules, and members who violate standards face
consequences.

Selection criteria include combat capability (obviously), but also
temperament. Good enforcers prefer resolving situations without
violence. Those who enjoy hurting people make poor enforcers, they
create problems rather than solving them.

Training emphasizes intimidation techniques, negotiation, and the
Guild's legal structure. Enforcers must understand rules thoroughly
enough to enforce them fairly.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Enforcers prefer intimidation to actual violence. Their presence is
often sufficient, people who see enforcers approaching tend to become
cooperative. When intimidation fails, they're capable of escalating
effectively.

They work in pairs or groups, backing each other and providing witnesses
for any actions taken. Solo enforcement is discouraged; it creates
situations without accountability.

When forced to fight, they're brutal and efficient. The Guild's
internal reputation requires that resisting enforcers be obviously
foolish. Those who try it receive object lessons that discourage future
resistance.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Enforcers occupy a complex position within Guild hierarchy. They're not
commanders, but they have authority that crosses normal chain of
command. This creates tension with captains who resent interference.

They maintain their own network, sharing information about trouble
spots, problematic members, and emerging issues. This intelligence
function is as important as their enforcement role.

Many enforcers are actually idealists who believe in the Guild's
system, they enforce rules because they think the rules are right.
Others are simply pragmatists who found a niche where their skills are
valued.

**Abilities:**

Enforcers can call on Guild resources for backup, other members will
respond to enforcement actions. This isn't special authority; it's
standard Guild protocol. Members who don't respond when enforcers call
face consequences.

Their intimidating presence can paralyze opposition through implied
threat of violence. This is trained capability, not supernatural power,
but it's remarkably effective.

**Cultural Significance:**

Enforcers represent the Guild's self-governance. Unlike national armies
that rely on external authority, the Guild polices itself. This
self-regulation is central to its reputation and independence.

They're controversial within the Guild. Some members appreciate the
order enforcers maintain. Others resent their authority and view them as
internal tyrants.

**Story Potential:**

-   Enforcers are investigating something that intersects with the
    party's activities

-   An enforcer needs outside help with an internal Guild matter

-   The party's actions have attracted enforcer attention

-   An enforcer believes a Guild member is being unjustly targeted and
    seeks allies

### 49.4 Contract Killer


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

Contract killers don't look like assassins. That's the point. They
look like merchants, servants, travelers, whatever cover their current
assignment requires. Their actual appearance varies; their ability to
appear unremarkable is constant.

When not undercover, they favor practical, dark clothing that blends
into shadows. Their weapons are concealable. Their movements are quiet
and controlled. Everything about them is optimized for not being noticed
until it's too late.

**Origins:**

The Guild officially doesn't employ assassins. Assassination is illegal
in most jurisdictions, and the Guild prefers to maintain plausible
legitimacy. Officially, contract killers don't exist.

Unofficially, certain specialized operatives handle "personal security
contracts" that sometimes require "preemptive neutralization of
threats." The language is careful. The results are fatal.

Selection draws from veterans who've demonstrated relevant
capabilities: stealth, patience, precision, and the ability to kill
without hesitation or remorse. Training is extensive and individualized.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Contract killers avoid fair fights entirely. Their goal is to eliminate
targets without detection, ideally without anyone knowing violence
occurred until well after the killer has departed.

They're meticulous planners who study targets extensively before
acting. They learn routines, identify vulnerabilities, and prepare
multiple contingency plans. Improvisation is a backup for when
preparation fails.

When forced into open combat, they're dangerous but not invincible.
Their skills are optimized for assassination, not battlefield fighting.
Smart contract killers retreat from fair fights rather than risk
failure.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Contract killers operate outside normal Guild hierarchy. They receive
assignments through specific channels and report to handlers rather than
captains. Most Guild members don't know who the killers are, which is
intentional.

They're solitary by necessity. Their work doesn't permit close
relationships. Most develop detached perspectives that allow them to
function, some might call it psychological damage.

Within their small community, they maintain professional respect for
skilled peers. Competence is the only currency that matters. Those who
fail don't survive to try again.

**Abilities:**

Contract killers are exceptional at killing from surprise. Their
training provides advantages against unaware targets and ensures that
ambush strikes are maximally lethal.

Their precision attack capability allows them to exploit vulnerabilities
in ways that normal fighters can't match. Combined with poisoned
weapons, they can eliminate targets far above their apparent combat
capability.

**Cultural Significance:**

Contract killers represent the darker side of mercenary work, the
services that everyone needs but no one wants to acknowledge. They're
the reason certain problems simply\... disappear.

Their existence is officially denied. This denial is conventional and
everyone involved understands it. The pretense maintains useful fictions
for employers and the Guild alike.

**Story Potential:**

-   A contract killer is targeting someone the party needs to protect

-   The party needs to locate and stop a killer before they complete an
    assignment

-   A contract killer seeks to leave the profession and needs help

-   The party must hire Guild services for an elimination they can't
    perform themselves

### 49.5 Iron Guild Captain


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

Captains look like what they are: successful mercenaries who've risen
through proven competence. Their equipment is exceptional, rewards of
successful contracts combined with Guild benefits. Their bearing
projects authority earned through demonstrated capability.

They're typically in their thirties or forties, old enough to have
accumulated experience, young enough to remain physically effective.
Scars and wear marks testify to the contracts they've survived.

**Origins:**

Captains command mercenary companies, typically fifty to two hundred
soldiers organized into squads and platoons. Reaching this position
requires demonstrated leadership capability in addition to personal
combat skill.

Selection comes from senior veterans who've shown aptitude for command.
The Guild promotes from within; outside recruitment at captain level is
extremely rare. This ensures captains understand Guild culture and
expectations.

Training for captaincy includes tactics, logistics, contract
negotiation, and personnel management. A captain's job is mostly
administrative; personal combat is a small fraction of their
responsibilities.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Captains lead from positions that maximize their effectiveness,
sometimes the front, sometimes the rear, depending on circumstances.
Their value is in command rather than personal fighting, but they're
entirely capable of direct combat when necessary.

They coordinate company operations: deployment, supply, discipline, and
contact with employers. A good captain keeps their company supplied,
paid, and pointed at appropriate targets.

In combat, their tactical leadership enhances everyone under their
command. Their presence doesn't just inspire, it coordinates, directing
efforts toward collective effectiveness.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Captains occupy middle management in Guild hierarchy. They answer to
senior leadership while commanding their own companies. This position
requires balancing upward expectations with downward responsibilities.

They compete with each other for prestigious contracts. Company
reputation depends largely on captain capability; captains work hard to
build and maintain their standing.

Most captains are intensely practical. They've risen through pragmatic
competence rather than idealism. They understand that the Guild exists
to profit from contracts, and they ensure their companies contribute to
that profit.

**Abilities:**

Captains provide tactical bonuses to everyone fighting under their
command. Their experience allows them to direct efforts effectively,
improving overall unit performance.

Their command capability allows coordinated actions, everyone striking
at once, everyone moving together. This coordination is the difference
between a mercenary company and a collection of individual fighters.

**Cultural Significance:**

Captains are the Guild's public faces. Employers deal with captains.
Authorities negotiate with captains. The Guild's reputation is built on
captain performance.

They represent mercenary work's legitimate aspirations: professional
soldiers commanding professional companies for professional purposes.
The more problematic aspects of the profession happen at other levels.

**Story Potential:**

-   A captain offers the party contract work as temporary additions to
    their company

-   The party must negotiate with a captain whose company blocks their
    path

-   A captain's past decisions create complications in the present

-   A captain suspects corruption within their own company and needs
    outside investigators

### 49.6 Guildmaster's Elite


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry)

**Physical Description:**

The Guildmaster's Elite are living legends. Their equipment is
masterwork or magical, accumulated over careers of exceptional
achievement. Their bearing projects absolute confidence earned through
decades of victory.

They're typically older than other active members, fifties or sixties,
but remain formidable through maintained training and (often) magical
assistance. What they've lost in youthful vigor, they've more than
replaced with experience and equipment.

Each Elite is recognizable. They have individual reputations built over
careers that span decades. Their names are known throughout the
mercenary profession.

**Origins:**

The Elite are selected from the best captains and specialists, those
who've demonstrated not just competence but excellence over extended
careers. There are never more than a dozen at any time.

Selection is by Guildmaster invitation only. Candidates have usually
declined earlier opportunities for promotion, preferring active service
to administrative roles. Eventually, the Guildmaster asks personally.

Their duties include protecting the Guildmaster, handling the Guild's
most sensitive and important contracts, and serving as final arbiters in
internal disputes. They're the Guild's ultimate authority after the
Guildmaster himself.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Elite fight with refined technique developed over decades. Every motion
is purposeful. Every attack is efficient. They've long since abandoned
flashy techniques in favor of what actually works.

They're remarkably difficult to defeat through psychological means.
Fear and charm effects that would disable lesser fighters simply don't
work, they've faced too much to be manipulated so easily.

Most prefer to end conflicts without combat if possible. They have
nothing to prove. Those who force them to fight rarely survive the
experience.

**Intelligence and Society:**

The Elite form the Guild's inner council, advising the Guildmaster on
policy and major decisions. Their collective experience represents
centuries of accumulated knowledge.

They maintain extensive networks built over career lifetimes. Former
colleagues, former employers, former enemies who became allies, their
contacts span Tirvandor.

Many struggle with mortality. They've achieved everything the
profession offers, yet time continues passing. What comes after being
the best is a question without comfortable answers.

**Abilities:**

Elite are exceptionally resilient. Their willpower allows them to
overcome failures through sheer determination, refusing to fall when
lesser warriors would be defeated.

Their mercenary's pride makes them nearly immune to mental
manipulation. Attempts to frighten or charm them typically fail.

Their commanding presence enhances allies' effectiveness, less through
tactical direction than through inspiring confidence by example.

**Cultural Significance:**

The Elite represent what mercenary careers can achieve. They're proof
that the profession leads somewhere, that excellence is recognized and
rewarded.

They're also reminders that even legends eventually age. How they
handle that transition, retiring gracefully, dying in service, or
declining into parody, shapes how younger members understand their own
futures.

**Story Potential:**

-   An Elite is assigned to a mission that intersects with the party's
    goals.

-   The party needs Elite-level capability for an impossible task.

-   An Elite's long history creates complications when old events
    resurface.

-   An aging Elite seeks a worthy final mission.

### 49.7 Garrick "Ironheart" Hammerfist


**Type:** Humanoid (dwarf), legendary craftsman-warrior

**Note:** *Garrick appears in the Monster Manual under Iron Guild
Mercenaries but is actually the founder of the Smiths' Guild, not the
Iron Guild. A full entry exists in Chapter 42: Goldreach NPCs (§42.3).
His connection to the Iron Guild stems from his legendary status in
Goldreach, where both organizations maintain headquarters, and his
occasional provision of weapons and equipment to Guild contracts.*

**Physical Description:**

Powerfully built even by dwarven standards, with arms like tree trunks
from over a century at the forge. His copper-red beard is braided with
metal rings, each representing a significant creation. Missing the last
two fingers of his left hand, a forge accident he refuses to discuss in
detail. His eyes are an unusual amber color that seems to glow near
flames.

**Why He Appears in Mercenary Contexts:**

Though Garrick is a master smith rather than a mercenary, his reputation
as a "legendary warrior and fair leader" comes from his younger years
before founding the Smiths' Guild. He served contracts, led expeditions
to recover rare materials, and fought in several significant conflicts.
His "Ironheart" nickname came from these adventures, not from the
steel defender he later created.

He maintains close ties with the Iron Guild because he supplies them
with weapons and armor. Senior Guild members still remember his active
service days. His fairness in dealings has earned respect across
mercenary communities.

**Current Role:**

Garrick is Guildmaster of the Smiths' Guild in Goldreach. He no longer
takes mercenary contracts but sometimes provides equipment, advice, or
crafting services to Iron Guild operations. His legendary status means
his endorsement carries weight in mercenary circles.

**Cross-Reference:**

See Chapter 42: Goldreach NPCs, §42.3 for Garrick's complete entry
including:

-   Full background and history

-   His masterwork creation "Ironheart" (the steel defender)

-   His connections to King Aldric IV and Archmagus Theron

-   His five major secrets including the dragon teacher and his wife's
    murder

-   His role as Smiths' Guild Guildmaster

*End of Chapter 44: Iron Guild Mercenaries*

## Chapter 50: Ascended-Touched


The Seven Ascended, the gods who emerged from mortal heroes during the
Worldrend, do not walk Tirvandor in person. Instead, they work through
chosen champions, blessed servants, and divine messengers who carry
their power and purpose into the mortal world.

These Ascended-Touched beings range from mortal champions blessed with
divine favor to celestial creatures directly created to serve divine
will. Each reflects their patron's nature: Thandros' champions enforce
law, Aethor's liberators break chains, Moira's seers glimpse fate, and
so on through the entire divine pantheon.

Not all touched by the divine remain faithful. Fallen Champions
represent the tragic potential when blessed heroes break their oaths or
succumb to corruption, their divine gifts twisted into something
terrible.

### 50.1 Blessed Paladin (General Ascended-Touched)


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry, divine champion)

**Physical Description:**

Blessed paladins radiate subtle divine presence. Their eyes occasionally
flash with inner light. Their voices carry undertones of authority that
transcend normal speech. They move with purpose that suggests divine
direction, not mechanically, but with the confidence of those who
believe their path is righteous.

Their equipment is typically well-maintained and often bears religious
symbols. Many wear the iconography of their patron Ascended prominently.
Some carry weapons or armor that glow faintly with divine power, gifts
from temples or supernatural sources.

**Origins:**

Blessed paladins are mortal champions who've received divine
recognition from one or more of the Seven Ascended. This blessing isn't
granted through ritual or application, it comes to those who've already
demonstrated the values their patron represents through action.

Some receive their blessing dramatically: visions, miraculous events,
direct divine intervention. Others realize gradually that their faith
has been recognized, noticing increasing effectiveness in prayer and
growing supernatural capability.

The blessing doesn't remove free will. Blessed paladins can still
choose their actions. However, actions that violate their patron's
principles may result in blessing withdrawal, temporarily or
permanently.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Blessed paladins fight with conviction that their cause is righteous.
This isn't arrogance but genuine belief, and it translates to combat
effectiveness. They're fearless not from inability to feel fear but
from faith that overcomes it.

In combat, they can channel divine energy through their weapons, causing
additional harm that seems to burn with holy light. This divine smite is
particularly effective against evil creatures, especially undead and
fiends.

They often lead from the front, inspiring others through example. Their
presence in a conflict signals that at least one of the Ascended has
interest in the outcome.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Blessed paladins occupy respected positions in most communities. Their
divine favor is recognized even by those who worship different Ascended,
the blessing itself validates their righteousness regardless of specific
patron.

Many struggle with the weight of expectation. Communities expect blessed
paladins to solve problems, mediate disputes, and exemplify virtue. This
pressure can be crushing, and some withdraw from society to serve in
less visible ways.

They maintain connections with temples and religious orders but aren't
necessarily members of formal hierarchies. Their authority comes from
divine recognition rather than institutional position.

**Abilities:**

Blessed paladins can channel divine energy through their attacks,
dealing additional radiant damage that represents their patron's power
manifest in the physical world.

Their divine connection provides some resistance to fear and mental
manipulation. The blessing seems to anchor their minds against
supernatural influence.

**Cultural Significance:**

Blessed paladins are living proof of divine attention. Their existence
confirms that the Ascended watch the mortal world and reward those who
embody divine values. This is theologically significant and practically
comforting.

Different cultures view them differently. Thaldros respects Thandros'
champions but views Aethor's liberators with suspicion. Aethoria
celebrates champions of freedom while questioning those who serve order
too rigidly. These tensions reflect the broader conflicts between
nations and faiths.

**Story Potential:**

-   A blessed paladin seeks help with a mission too large for individual
    effort

-   The party must convince a paladin that their cause is righteous

-   A paladin's blessing is wavering due to moral complications

-   Someone is falsely claiming paladin status for personal gain

### 50.2 Thandros' Justicar


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry, divine champion of Thandros)

**Physical Description:**

Justicars embody law's implacable nature. They dress in formal attire
that suggests judicial authority, robes, chains of office, or armor
marked with Thandros' scales-and-gavel symbol. Their expressions are
stern, their bearing formal, their movements precise.

Their equipment often includes judicial implements: weighted symbols
representing law's authority, formal documents, and the Mace of Justice
that serves as both weapon and badge of office. Their presence commands
attention and demands respect for proper procedure.

**Origins:**

Justicars are chosen by Thandros from among those who've demonstrated
unwavering commitment to law and justice. Many are former judges,
magistrates, or lawyers who pursued justice through legitimate systems.
Others are investigators who uncovered corruption, or enforcers who
maintained order fairly.

The calling comes through dreams of law courts where Thandros himself
presides. Those who accept the calling find themselves compelled to
pursue justice wherever it's denied. Those who refuse return to normal
lives, but the offer is rarely extended twice.

Training emphasizes both combat and legal knowledge. Justicars must
understand law deeply enough to enforce it justly, and fight effectively
enough to overcome those who resist lawful authority.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Justicars prefer to resolve situations through proper legal procedure.
They investigate, gather evidence, pronounce judgment, and only then
enforce sentences. Violence is a last resort when law has been properly
applied and defied.

In combat, their weapons strike with particular force against those
guilty of crimes, as if Thandros himself judges through the blow. Their
Gavel Strike can temporarily stun opponents, a physical manifestation of
law's paralyzing authority.

They're not cruel or sadistic. Justice, in Thandros' understanding, is
about proper order, not punishment for its own sake. Justicars enforce
law; they don't enjoy doing so.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Justicars work within legal systems when possible, supplementing secular
authorities rather than replacing them. They advise judges, investigate
complex cases, and handle matters beyond normal law enforcement's
capability.

They're controversial figures. Those who believe in law appreciate
their incorruptibility. Those who've suffered under unjust laws see
them as enforcers of oppression. Justicars themselves wrestle with this
tension, they serve Law, but not all laws are just.

Most recognize the difference between law and justice, and struggle when
the two conflict. Some resolve this by working to change unjust laws;
others enforce law regardless and trust that proper procedure will
eventually correct injustice.

**Abilities:**

The Mace of Justice deals additional divine damage against those who've
committed crimes, as if guilt itself makes one vulnerable to law's
enforcement.

Their Gavel Strike can temporarily incapacitate opponents, a moment
where judgment renders the guilty unable to act, frozen by law's
authority.

**Cultural Significance:**

In Thaldros, Justicars are respected agents of proper order. The
Empire's legal system, whatever its flaws, represents genuine attempt
at fair governance, and Justicars embody that ideal.

In Aethoria, they're viewed with suspicion as potential tyrants. Law
can be used to oppress, and Aethorian culture emphasizes that unjust
laws deserve defiance rather than enforcement.

**Story Potential:**

-   A Justicar investigates something that intersects with the party's
    activities

-   The party must prove their innocence to a Justicar pursuing them

-   A Justicar recognizes that law and justice conflict and seeks
    guidance

-   Someone the party needs is in Justicar custody awaiting judgment

### 50.3 Aethor's Liberator


**Type:** Celestial (divine servant of Aethor)

**Physical Description:**

Aethor's Liberators are celestial beings created directly by the god of
freedom. They appear as beautiful humanoids with luminous features and
wings of golden light. Their faces express boundless compassion and
fierce determination in equal measure.

They can assume mortal forms to move undetected, but their true nature
often shows in small ways: chains rust in their presence, locked doors
tend to swing open, and caged creatures grow calm when they pass.

**Origins:**

Liberators are celestial servants created by Aethor rather than promoted
from mortal champions. They exist specifically to break chains, free
prisoners, and liberate the oppressed. Each Liberator represents
Aethor's ongoing commitment to freedom.

They appear in Tirvandor when Aethor's attention is drawn to particular
situations of bondage or oppression. This might be a single unjust
imprisonment or systematic enslavement of entire populations. The
Liberator arrives, acts, and departs when freedom is achieved.

Their presence is rare, Aethor sends Liberators for significant
interventions rather than every instance of injustice. Most oppression
must be overcome by mortals themselves; Liberators address situations
beyond mortal capability.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Liberators prefer to free captives without violence when possible.
They're diplomatic, persuasive, and willing to negotiate. Their goal is
liberation, not punishment of oppressors, though they'll fight if
necessary.

When combat is required, they're devastating opponents. Their weapons
burn with freedom's light, and their ability to instantly break all
bonds makes them nearly impossible to capture or restrain.

They can change shape to infiltrate prisons, approach captors without
suspicion, or escape pursuit. This shapeshifting serves their liberating
mission rather than personal preference.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Liberators operate independently, following Aethor's guidance rather
than mortal authority. They respect those who work toward freedom but
don't subordinate themselves to mortal movements or organizations.

They communicate telepathically and can understand any language, freedom
transcends linguistic barriers. Their conversations often focus on the
nature of freedom, the causes of oppression, and the possibilities of
liberation.

They don't hate oppressors the way mortals might. They see slavers and
tyrants as obstacles to freedom rather than personal enemies. This
perspective sometimes frustrates mortals who want righteous vengeance.

**Abilities:**

Liberators can instantly free anyone from any restraint, magical or
mundane, within their presence. Chains shatter, locks spring open, and
magical bindings dissolve.

Their presence provides allies with resistance to mental compulsion and
fear. Freedom, in their company, extends beyond physical restraint to
psychological liberation as well.

**Cultural Significance:**

In Aethoria, Liberators are beloved messengers of their patron god.
Their appearances are celebrated as divine confirmation of Aethorian
values. Stories of Liberator interventions inspire continued resistance
against oppression.

In Thaldros, they're viewed as dangerous subversives who undermine
proper order. Their ability to free prisoners and slaves threatens
social structures that Thaldros considers legitimate.

**Story Potential:**

-   A Liberator arrives to free someone the party needs to remain
    captive

-   The party must locate a Liberator for a liberation beyond their
    capability

-   A Liberator's intervention creates political complications the
    party must navigate

-   The party witnesses a Liberator's appearance and must decide how to
    respond

### 50.4 Moira's Seer


**Type:** Humanoid (any ancestry, divine prophet of Moira)

**Physical Description:**

Moira's Seers look perpetually distracted, their eyes focused on things
others cannot see. They dress in practical but often mismatched
clothing, fashion matters little when you can see possible futures. Many
have prematurely gray or white hair, as if witnessing too many
possibilities ages them.

Their eyes are their most notable feature: often clouded, occasionally
glowing, sometimes seeming to look through rather than at whoever
they're addressing. They speak in tenses that don't quite match the
present, and their conversations often include references to events that
haven't happened yet.

**Origins:**

Seers are chosen by Moira, goddess of fate, from among those who already
demonstrate unusual sensitivity to time and possibility. Some have
prophetic dreams from childhood. Others develop prescience after
traumatic events. Moira formalizes and enhances abilities that already
existed in potential.

The calling comes through visions of the Weaver's Loom, where Moira
tends the threads of fate. Those who accept learn to read the threads
themselves, imperfectly, partially, but genuinely. Those who refuse
retain whatever natural sensitivity they had but don't develop further.

Training emphasizes interpretation rather than simple sight. Seeing
possibilities is relatively easy; understanding what they mean and which
might come to pass is the seer's true art.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Seers avoid direct combat when possible. Their value lies in knowledge,
not violence. They prefer to share information that allows others to
make better choices rather than intervening directly.

When forced to fight, they use their prescience defensively, glimpsing
incoming attacks and avoiding them. Their Prophetic Vision can overwhelm
opponents with visions of possible futures, incapacitating them through
information overload.

They're frustratingly cryptic even when trying to be clear. The nature
of prophecy resists direct statement; the future changes when described,
and seers learn to communicate in ways that preserve possibility rather
than constraining it.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Seers occupy uncertain social positions. Everyone wants to know the
future; few appreciate the complexity of actually knowing it. Seers are
constantly pressured to provide simple predictions for complex
situations.

Many live as hermits or recluses, limiting contact with those who would
demand impossible clarity. Others serve as advisors to leaders willing
to accept ambiguity. A few become frauds, providing the simple
predictions people want rather than the complicated truths they see.

They maintain connections with each other, sharing techniques for
managing the burden of sight. These informal networks span political
boundaries, prophecy doesn't care about nations.

**Abilities:**

Seers can share visions with others, potentially overwhelming them with
possible futures. This is usually defensive, attackers caught in
prophetic vision can't act effectively, but can also be used to
communicate complex information.

Their Weaver's Warning allows them to grant others brief prescience,
providing a second chance at important moments when fate might have gone
poorly.

**Cultural Significance:**

Seers are respected across Tirvandor as genuine prophets. Their
predictions don't always come true, prophecy is probability rather than
certainty, but they're accurate often enough to be valued.

They're also figures of some suspicion. Those who know the future might
manipulate events toward preferred outcomes. Seers' cryptic
communication style doesn't help; it's easy to suspect they're hiding
something.

**Story Potential:**

-   A Seer provides cryptic guidance that only makes sense later

-   The party must protect a Seer from those who would exploit prophetic
    gifts

-   A Seer's prediction threatens to become self-fulfilling in negative
    ways

-   The party seeks a Seer for information about future events

### 50.5 Sylvara's Wild Hunter


**Type:** Fey (divine servant of Sylvara)

**Physical Description:**

Wild Hunters are fey beings who serve Sylvara, goddess of nature and the
wild. They appear as lithe, fierce humanoids with features suggesting
various predatory animals, wolf-like eyes, antlered brows, or fingers
that end in subtle claws. Leaves and vines often grow directly from
their skin, and their hair moves like living things.

They're naturally camouflaged in wild environments, their appearance
shifting to blend with their surroundings. In forests, they're dappled
with green and brown; in tundra, pale as snow; in desert, tawny and
sun-bleached.

**Origins:**

Wild Hunters are fey created by Sylvara to protect the natural world
from those who would destroy it. They're not reformed mortals but
beings born of divine will and wild magic, shaped to serve as nature's
defenders.

They appear where the wild is threatened: forests being clear-cut,
rivers being poisoned, ecosystems being destroyed. Their arrival signals
that nature itself is fighting back, that Sylvara has taken notice of
offense against her domain.

Individual Wild Hunters persist for centuries, becoming tied to
particular regions they protect. Some are almost worshipped by local
communities as forest spirits or nature gods.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Wild Hunters judge mortals by their relationship with nature. Those who
respect the wild receive guidance and protection. Those who harm it face
relentless pursuit, Wild Hunters never forget offenses against nature
and never stop hunting until balance is restored.

In combat, they're fierce and mobile, using their speed and
environmental knowledge to maximum advantage. They fight with
lightning-charged weapons and can summon wolves or other predators to
assist. Their Lightning Leap ability makes them nearly impossible to
corner or trap.

They're not evil or sadistic, they don't enjoy killing. But they're
absolutely dedicated to nature's protection and will destroy threats
without hesitation or remorse.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Wild Hunters understand mortal speech and customs but don't share
mortal values. Civilization itself isn't evil to them, they recognize
that some mortal settlements exist in balance with nature. It's
destruction they oppose, not presence.

They communicate in terms that emphasize natural cycles, predator-prey
relationships, and ecological balance. Their perspective is genuinely
alien to most mortals, focused on species and ecosystems rather than
individuals.

They maintain loose connections with each other and with other fey,
sharing information about threats and coordinating responses to
large-scale environmental destruction.

**Abilities:**

Wild Hunters can summon predatory animals to fight alongside them,
calling wolves, bears, or other appropriate creatures depending on
environment.

Their Lightning Leap allows them to teleport short distances, leaving
electrical discharge behind, making them extraordinarily mobile and
nearly impossible to pin down.

Their weapons channel storm energy, dealing lightning damage in addition
to physical harm.

**Cultural Significance:**

In rural communities, Wild Hunters are respected and feared as genuine
forces of nature. Farmers and hunters who maintain traditional practices
that respect ecological balance may receive Wild Hunter protection;
those who over-hunt or over-harvest may find themselves targets.

Urban populations generally don't encounter Wild Hunters directly, but
stories of their wrath serve as cultural reminders about nature's
power.

**Story Potential:**

-   A Wild Hunter is pursuing someone the party needs to protect

-   The party must gain Wild Hunter approval to enter protected
    wilderness

-   Environmental destruction threatens to summon Wild Hunter response

-   A Wild Hunter seeks mortal help with a threat too large for
    individual response

### 50.6 Sera's Mercy


**Type:** Celestial (divine messenger of Sera)

**Physical Description:**

Sera's Mercies are small celestial beings, typically appearing as
luminous children or diminutive winged figures radiating gentle light.
Their features are soft and compassionate, their expressions conveying
profound empathy and kindness.

They glow with warm, healing light that intensifies when they use their
powers. Their presence brings feelings of comfort and safety, even in
dangerous situations, those near a Mercy feel strangely calm.

**Origins:**

Mercies are celestial servants created by Sera, goddess of healing and
compassion. They exist to ease suffering wherever it occurs, healing the
wounded, comforting the dying, and offering hope to the despairing.

They appear in Tirvandor during times of great suffering: plagues,
disasters, wars. Their presence doesn't prevent suffering but makes it
bearable, ensuring that divine compassion accompanies mortal pain.

Individual Mercies may linger in particular locations, hospitals,
temples, sites of ongoing tragedy, providing continuous care for as long
as suffering continues.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Mercies avoid violence almost absolutely. They're healers, not
fighters. Their touch heals the living and provides comfort to the
dying; only undead suffer from their presence, as their healing energy
becomes destructive to creatures animated by negative energy.

When threatened, they use their Peaceful Presence to defuse violence,
calming aggressive individuals into temporary peace. If this fails, they
flee rather than fight, their purpose is healing, not combat.

They treat all suffering equally. A Mercy will heal wounded enemies as
readily as wounded allies, seeing pain rather than allegiance. This
sometimes frustrates those who would use them as tactical assets.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Mercies communicate telepathically in any language, conveying emotion as
much as words. They speak of suffering, healing, hope, and comfort,
their vocabulary is shaped by their purpose.

They don't judge those they help. Their compassion extends to everyone:
heroes and villains, saints and sinners. Some mortals find this
troubling, shouldn't divine beings distinguish between deserving and
undeserving suffering?

Sera's theology answers that all suffering deserves compassion. Mercies
embody this principle absolutely.

**Abilities:**

Their Touch of Mercy heals the wounded or harms undead, the same energy
that restores life destroys its mockery.

Their Shield of Compassion can temporarily protect individuals from
harm, extending Sera's protection to those in immediate danger.

Their Peaceful Presence can calm entire groups, temporarily suppressing
violence and aggression.

**Cultural Significance:**

Mercies are universally beloved across Tirvandor. Even nations at war
welcome their presence on battlefields, knowing that Mercies will heal
both sides without discrimination.

Their impartiality occasionally creates problems. When a Mercy heals a
notorious villain or comforts a dying tyrant, some question whether
compassion should extend so far. Sera's faithful argue that if
compassion has limits, it isn't truly compassion.

**Story Potential:**

-   A Mercy is healing someone the party needs to capture

-   The party must protect a Mercy from those who would exploit or
    destroy it

-   A Mercy's presence in an unexpected location raises questions

-   The party seeks a Mercy for healing beyond normal capability

### 50.7 Mordain's Sentinel


**Type:** Undead (divine guardian of Mordain)

**Physical Description:**

Mordain's Sentinels are undead warriors animated by divine will rather
than necromantic magic. They wear ancient armor, typically from the era
when they died, and carry weapons of equal antiquity. Their forms are
skeletal or desiccated but project power rather than horror.

Their eye sockets glow with cold white light, not the malevolent fire of
evil undead, but the steady radiance of duty fulfilled. They move with
military precision, and their presence is solemn rather than terrifying.

**Origins:**

Sentinels are warriors who died protecting sacred sites, fulfilling
oaths, or serving Mordain's principles of honor and proper death.
Rather than passing to the afterlife, they received Mordain's blessing
to continue their service as eternal guardians.

This isn't necromancy in the usual sense. Sentinels aren't bound to
undeath against their will, they chose to remain, and Mordain's power
sustains them. They could pass on if they wished; they remain because
their duty isn't complete.

They guard tombs, temples, sacred battlefields, and other sites
significant to the cycle of death and memory. Their presence ensures
that the dead are honored and the living respect proper boundaries.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Sentinels guard rather than attack. They challenge those who approach
their sites, determining whether visitors deserve access. Those who
demonstrate proper respect may pass; those who don't face resistance.

In combat, they're formidable, ancient warriors with centuries of
experience and complete immunity to fear, fatigue, and psychological
manipulation. Their weapons deal necrotic damage representing death's
touch.

They can command other undead within their territory, organizing
defensive forces against intruders. They can also temporarily animate
the dead to assist in protection, not creating permanent undead but
calling spirits to temporary service.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Sentinels retain full intelligence from their living days, often
enhanced by centuries of contemplation. They're excellent sources of
historical information, having witnessed events that living memory has
lost.

They're lonely figures, separated from living society by their nature.
Many appreciate visitors who treat them as individuals rather than
obstacles, engaging in conversation before (or instead of) combat.

They maintain communication with other Sentinels through mysterious
means, sharing information about threats and coordinating responses to
desecration attempts.

**Abilities:**

Their weapons deal necrotic damage as well as physical, the touch of
death itself accompanying each blow.

Their Sentinel's Command can enhance other undead in their territory,
coordinating defensive forces.

Their Honor the Fallen ability can temporarily call spirits of the dead
to assist in protecting sacred sites.

**Cultural Significance:**

Sentinels are respected as honorable guardians rather than feared as
monsters. Communities near Sentinel-protected sites maintain proper
relationships with them, providing offerings and maintenance for guarded
tombs in exchange for protection.

They represent the possibility of meaningful existence after death, not
the horror of undeath but its potential nobility. Mordain's theology
emphasizes that death is transition rather than ending, and Sentinels
embody this principle.

**Story Potential:**

-   A Sentinel guards something the party needs to access

-   The party must negotiate passage through Sentinel territory

-   A Sentinel's ancient knowledge is essential for understanding
    current events

-   A Sentinel seeks help protecting its site from threats beyond its
    capability

### 50.8 Fallen Champion


**Type:** Undead (corrupted divine champion)

**Physical Description:**

Fallen Champions retain the bearing of the heroes they once were, but
corruption has twisted their features. Their armor is tarnished or
rusted, their weapons darkened, their eyes burning with bitter fire
rather than divine light.

They radiate despair rather than hope, an aura of failure and corruption
that affects everyone nearby. Their presence feels wrong in ways that
transcend physical appearance, as if reality itself rejects what
they've become.

**Origins:**

Fallen Champions were once blessed paladins or divine champions who
broke their oaths, succumbed to corruption, or betrayed the principles
that earned their blessing. Their fall didn't simply remove divine
favor, it twisted it into something terrible.

The fall can happen many ways: desperation that led to forbidden
actions, gradual compromise that eventually crossed uncrossable lines,
deliberate betrayal for power or revenge. Whatever the cause, the result
is the same: blessed champions become cursed monsters.

Some fell centuries ago and continue their corrupted existence. Others
are recent, their fall a tragedy that those who knew them still mourn.

**Behavior and Combat:**

Fallen Champions are driven by bitterness and resentment. They hate what
they were, hate those who remain faithful, and hate the divine beings
whose standards they couldn't meet. This hatred fuels their violence.

In combat, they're dangerous opponents, retaining combat skills from
their champion days but adding necrotic power from their corrupted
state. Their Corrupted Smite mirrors the divine smite they once wielded,
but deals necrotic rather than radiant damage.

Their Aura of Despair affects everyone nearby, projecting their own
hopelessness outward. Those caught in this aura may find themselves
unable to move, paralyzed by the Fallen Champion's communicated
despair.

**Intelligence and Society:**

Fallen Champions retain their intelligence but their perspective is
warped by corruption. They remember their former ideals but now see them
as naive or foolish. They remember their former allies but now view them
as enemies or fools.

Some serve dark powers that contributed to their fall. Others operate
independently, pursuing personal vendettas or nihilistic destruction. A
few desperately seek redemption while fearing it's impossible.

They're usually solitary, though some gather followers among those
attracted to their power or convinced by their bitter philosophy.

**Abilities:**

Fallen Champions deal necrotic damage through weapons once blessed with
divine power, their curse transforming holy might into unholy
destruction.

Their Aura of Despair can paralyze opponents with communicated
hopelessness, making them unable to act or even flee.

Their Corrupted Smite adds massive necrotic damage to attacks, a twisted
mirror of the divine smite they once wielded righteously.

**Cultural Significance:**

Fallen Champions are cautionary tales. Their existence reminds the
faithful that even blessed heroes can fall, that righteousness requires
constant vigilance, and that no one is immune to corruption's
temptation.

They're also tragedies, people who once served divine purpose reduced
to monsters. Many who encounter Fallen Champions feel sorrow alongside
fear, mourning what was lost as much as fearing what remains.

**Story Potential:**

-   A Fallen Champion from a party member's past resurfaces

-   The party must stop a champion in the process of falling

-   A Fallen Champion seeks redemption and approaches the party for help

-   Information about current threats lies in a Fallen Champion's
    corrupted memories

*End of Chapter 45: Ascended-Touched*
